query: Has anyone used small-batch ultrasonic atomization (for example an AMAZEMET rePOWDER or a 3D Lab ATO Lab / ATO One, or any laboratory ultrasonic atomizer) to make powders of NEW or custom aluminium alloy compositions and then processed those powders by laser powder bed fusion (LPBF / SLM) and measured mechanical properties, as part of an alloy development or alloy screening workflow? Please list every such study for aluminium alloys (and, separately, the closest examples for other alloy systems), with the compositions made, batch size, atomizer settings (frequency, melt temperature, plate/sonotrode), powder size distribution and yield in the LPBF size range, composition accuracy versus target (loss of Mg, Zn, etc.), the LPBF machine and parameters, and the properties obtained. Also say whether any study has coupled such a small-batch powder route to Bayesian optimization, machine learning or an autonomous / closed-loop alloy design workflow, and how many compositions were made.
task_summary: Survey Of Small Batch Ultrasonic Atomized Aluminum Powders For LPBF Parameters Properties And Closed Integration

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available
        - NO_LONGER_AVAILABLE: No longer available
        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening
        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research
        - BASIC_SCIENCE: Basic Science
        - DEVICE_FEASIBILITY: Device Feasibility

    InterventionType:
        - BEHAVIORAL: Behavioral interventions

to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: Has anyone used small-batch ultrasonic atomization (for example an AMAZEMET rePOWDER or a 3D Lab ATO Lab / ATO One, or any laboratory ultrasonic atomizer) to make powders of NEW or custom aluminium alloy compositions and then processed those powders by laser powder bed fusion (LPBF / SLM) and measured mechanical properties, as part of an alloy development or alloy screening workflow? Please list every such study for aluminium alloys (and, separately, the closest examples for other alloy systems), with the compositions made, batch size, atomizer settings (frequency, melt temperature, plate/sonotrode), powder size distribution and yield in the LPBF size range, composition accuracy versus target (loss of Mg, Zn, etc.), the LPBF machine and parameters, and the properties obtained. Also say whether any study has coupled such a small-batch powder route to Bayesian optimization, machine learning or an autonomous / closed-loop alloy design workflow, and how many compositions were made.

Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.

Abstract:
Abstract. This article investigates the processing and characterization of iron aluminide lightweight alloy by plasma ultrasonic atomization and laser powder based directed energy deposition (DED-LB/p) and its comparison with other additive manufacturing alternatives. DED-LB/p provides precisely controllable process parameters, a wide range of feed materials supplied in powder form, a relatively high deposition rate and low heat input. These features favor the DED - LB/p process for novel materials such as iron aluminide. Thanks to a combination of desirable properties such as low density, high specific strength, low material cost, excellent oxidation resistance, and corrosion resistance, Fe-Al has established considerable potential to replace high-alloy chromium steels and, in some cases, even superalloys in high-temperature applications. In this study, Fe-Al alloy was first atomized into powder form from a commercial rod with core of aluminum and sleeve of a commercial low alloy-steel by plasma ultrasonic atomization. The resulting powder was then used for additive manufacturing with DED-LB/p in order to reduce cost and analyze the process chain. The results show that the use of powder produced by plasma ultrasonic atomization from commercial raw materials in the DED-LB/p process provides an effective combination for additive manufacturing of Fe-Al alloy and has some advantages over the alternative WAAM method.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Throughout recent years, the implementation of nanoparticles into the microstructure of additively manufactured (AM) parts has gained great attention in the material science community. The dispersion strengthening (DS) effect achieved leads to a substantial improvement in the mechanical properties of the alloy used. In this work, an ex situ approach of powder conditioning prior to the AM process as per a newly developed fluidized bed reactor (FBR) was applied to a titanium-enriched variant of the NiCu-based Alloy 400. Powders were investigated before and after FBR exposure, and it was found that the conditioning led to a significant increase in the TiN formation along grain boundaries. Manufactured to parts via laser-based powder bed fusion of metals (PBF-LB/M), the ex situ FBR approach not only revealed a superior microstructure compared to unconditioned parts but also with respect to a recently introduced in situ approach based on a gas atomization reaction synthesis (GARS). A substantially higher number of nanoparticles formed along cell walls and enabled an effective suppression of dislocation movement, resulting in excellent tensile, creep, and fatigue properties, even at elevated temperatures up to 750 °C. Such outstanding properties have never been documented for AM-processed Alloy 400, which is why the demonstrated FBR ex situ conditioning marks a promising modification route for future alloy systems.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>(TiH2 + ScH3)/Al-Mg composite powders with different Ti contents were produced by ball milling. These composite powders were fabricated to cube and cuboid shape samples via a laser powder bed fusion process with optimal processing parameters. The TiH2 and ScH3 particles underwent dehydrogenation during the laser powder bed fusion process, and these composite powders ultimately formed Al-Mg-Sc-Ti alloys. The relative density, printability, microstructure, hardness and tensile properties of these alloy samples were investigated. The results show that these Al-Mg-Sc-Ti alloys have lower hot-crack sensitivity, having fine equiaxed grains. An Al18Mg3(Ti,Sc)2 intermetallic phase and in situ L12-Al3(Sc,Ti) precipitations formed during the laser powder bed fusion process, which is beneficial for nucleation and dispersion strengthening. The ultimate tensile strength of the Al-Mg-0.7Sc-1.0Ti alloy was 313.6 MPa with an elongation of 6.6%. During the hot isostatic pressing treatment, most of the Mg element precipitated from the matrix and changed the Al3(Sc,Ti) into a Al18Mg3(Ti,Sc)2 precipitate completely. The Al-Mg-Sc-Ti alloys were nearly fully dense after the hot isostatic pressing treatment and exhibited better mechanical properties. The ultimate tensile strength of the Al-Mg-0.7Sc-1.0Ti was 475 MPa with an elongation of 8.5%.</jats:p>

Abstract:
A new powder production method has been developed to speed up the search for novel alloys for additive manufacturing. The technique involves an ultrasonically agitated cold crucible installed at the top of a 20 kHz ultrasonic sonotrode. The material is melted with an electric arc and undergoes pulverization with standing wave vibrations. Several different alloys in various forms, including noble and metallic glass alloys, were chosen to test the process. The atomized particles showed exceptional sphericity, while powder output suitable for additive manufacturing reached up to 60%. The AMZ4 metallic glass powder remained amorphous below the 50 μm fraction, while tungsten addition led to crystallization in each fraction. Minor contamination and high Mn and Zn evaporation, especially in the finest particles, was observed in atomized powders. The innovative ultrasonic atomization method appears as a promising tool for material scientists to develop powders with tailored chemical composition, size and structure.

Abstract:
The quality and properties of metal powders are essential for powder metallurgical (PM) processes in general and for additive manufacturing (AM) processing routes in particular. Thus, a variety of atomization technologies were established meeting the multiple needs of the different processing technologies. However, the production of refractory metal alloy powder remains challenging due to their high liquidus temperatures (>2000 °C), the formation of brittle intermetallic phases, as well as the reactivity with and sensitivity to interstitials of the constituting elements. In this contribution, powders made of Mo-20Si-52.8-Ti (at.%) were produced by a novel ultrasonic atomization (UA) process at laboratory-scale using an industrial electrode induction gas atomization (EIGA) process with a modified electrode concept for the first time. UA allows flexibility in alloy composition due to the arc melting-based principle, while the EIGA electrode is PM manufactured from elemental powders to provide similar flexibility on a larger scale. The powders resulting from these two processes were compared with respect to size distribution, sphericity, microstructure and phase constitution, chemical composition, and interstitial impurity content. In addition, several powder batches were produced with the UA process in order to assess the process reliability and stability. The properties, quality, and quantities of UA powders perfectly meet the requests for alloy development for powder bed fusion AM, while the modified EIGA process allows the upscaling of the alloy powder quantities.

Abstract:
The adoption of additive manufacturing (AM) has driven extensive research into metal feedstocks, uncovering strong links between powder quality and the performance of printed parts. Poor powder characteristics, inadequate flowability or inconsistent packing, can significantly degrade the mechanical performance of the final 3D-printed components. This study investigates the effects of arc manipulator angle, electrical current, and vibration amplitude on AlSi12 powder quality via ultrasonic atomization (UA). Parameter adjustments significantly influenced particle size distribution, with span variations up to 37.5%. Optimal rheological properties were achieved by increasing the vibration amplitude (from 75 to 80%), decreasing the arc angle (from 5° to -5°), and reducing the current (from 150 A to 140 A). A modified AM suitability factor (AMS) was developed, incorporating logarithmic transformation and custom weighting to mitigate high-uncertainty parameter effects. Results revealed a non-linear relationship between powder suitability and arc angle, with a sharp worsening above 0°. Electrical current had the greatest impact on powder quality, followed by arc angle and vibration amplitude. Benchmarking showed that UA powder achieved suitability factors 21% higher than commercial powder, with improved sphericity compared to the irregular, fused particles of commercial alternatives. These findings underscore the potential of UA to enhance AM part reliability.

Abstract:
Specimens of a medium-entropy Fe65(CoNi)25Cr9.5C0.5 (in at.%) alloy were produced using additive manufacturing (selective laser melting, SLM). The selected parameters of SLM resulted in a very high density in the specimens with a residual porosity of less than 0.5%. The structure and mechanical behavior of the alloy were studied under tension at room and cryogenic temperatures. The microstructure of the alloy produced by SLM comprised an elongated substructure, inside which cells with a size of ~300 nm were observed. The as-produced alloy demonstrated high yield strength and ultimate tensile strength (YS = 680 MPa; UTS = 1800 MPa) along with good ductility (tensile elongation = 26%) at a cryogenic temperature (77 K) that was associated with the development of transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) effect. At room temperature, the TRIP effect was less pronounced. Consequently, the alloy demonstrated lower strain hardening and a YS/UTS of 560/640 MPa. The deformation mechanisms of the alloy are discussed.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Sustainable feedstock management remains a major challenge in laser beam powder bed fusion (PBF-LB), where conventional reuse strategies are typically limited to sieving and blending rather than full material regeneration. Ultrasonic atomization (UA) offers a fundamentally different powder production route based on capillary-wave instabilities induced at the surface of a molten metal by high-frequency vibrations. In contrast to turbulence-driven atomization, droplet formation in UA is primarily governed by ultrasonic frequency and intrinsic thermophysical properties of the melt, enabling quasi-deterministic particle formation with high sphericity and reduced satellite formation. In this study, ultrasonic atomization was investigated as a closed-loop route for converting PBF-LB-manufactured 316L stainless steel parts into reusable powder. Printed rods were remelted and atomized under controlled variation of electric current and vibration amplitude. The resulting powders were characterized in terms of morphology, internal microstructure, particle size distribution, chemical composition, and gas impurity content. UA produced highly spherical particles with reduced internal porosity and improved flowability compared to the initial gas-atomized powder, while preserving the principal alloying elements. An increase in oxygen content was observed after recycling, attributed to selective high-temperature oxidation under residual oxygen in nominally inert conditions. The results establish a mechanistic framework for transforming consolidated PBF-LB material into secondary feedstock and identify key parameters governing structural and compositional stability in closed-loop recycling.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Recycling of titanium alloys represents a modern and economically attractive processing route, as it enables a significant reduction in production costs associated with the high price of titanium. However, the properties of recycled β-titanium alloys have not yet been sufficiently investigated in the scientific literature, and their potential for processing by additive manufacturing technologies remains largely unexplored. This study focuses on evaluating the recycling of Ti-15Mo and Ti-13Nb-13Zr alloys using the horizontal plasma arc melting (HPAM) method and further examines subsequent processing steps, including hot working to the required shape for atomisation and subsequent powder processing via the LPBF technique. In all technological stages, the microstructure was characterised, chemical analysis was performed, and, where applicable, mechanical properties were evaluated. The results demonstrate that recycling of the investigated alloys is feasible, as is their subsequent processing up to the production of additively manufactured specimens. Nevertheless, strict control of the oxygen content is critical for both alloys, as the current levels exceed the limits specified by the relevant standards. At such elevated oxygen concentrations, the alloys are unsuitable for biomedical applications; however, their use in structural applications remains realistic, particularly considering the production cost reduction achieved through the implementation of recycling.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>A Ti–6Al–7Nb–0.3Y spherical powder was produced by ultrasonic atomization (UA), and its < 63 µm (d50 ≈ 53 µm) and 63–125 µm (d50 ≈ 82 µm) fractions were characterized for laser powder-bed fusion (LPBF) of patient–specific biomedical implants. Both fractions show near-ideal sphericity (1.01) with no satellites or internal pores, flow times of 26.8–28.0 s/50 g and bulk densities of 2.35–2.45 g/cm3 (51–53% of true density), matching commercial powder-bed feedstocks. XRD revealed only hexagonal α(α′)-Ti with a microstrain of 0.45–0.55%. Nanoindentation showed a hardness of 4.55–4.90 GPa, exceeding that of laser-powder-bed-fused Ti–6Al–4V (3.66 GPa), and an elastic modulus of 119–148 GPa on rigidly supported particles. Simultaneous thermal analysis showed stability up to 450 °C in all atmospheres, oxidation in air above 720 °C (Ea ≈ 160–170 kJ/mol) and mass gains at 1195 °C of 23.2–25.7% (air), 4.9–6.8% (N2) and 1.7–2.1% (Ar). The Ti–6Al–7Nb–0.3Y powder contains 0.69–0.74 wt.% Oxygen, far beyond the scavenging capacity of the retained 0.11–0.12 wt.% Yttrium, as well as 0.09–0.12 wt.% Nitrogen and 0.013–0.015 wt.% Hydrogen.</jats:p>

With most powders being imported and expensive, there is need to locally produce powder from extracted metal, scrap materials and used powders for additive manufacturing. "10.3390/app15042221", url = "https://doi.org/10.3390/app15042221", publisher = "MDPI AG", issue = "4", issn = "2076-3417" } Abstract: The manufacturing sector is a major contributor to global energy consumption and greenhouse gas emissions, positioning sustainability as a critical priority. Aluminum, valued for its lightweight and recyclable properties, plays a vital role in advancing energy-efficient solutions across transportation and aerospace industries. The processing of aluminum alloys through laser-based powder bed fusion of metals (PBF-LB/M), a cutting-edge additive manufacturing technology, enhances sustainability by optimizing material usage and enabling innovative lightweight designs. Based on the published literature, the present study analyzed the ecological impacts of aluminum PBF-LB/M manufacturing through life cycle assessment, circular economy principles, and eco-design strategies, identifying opportunities to reduce environmental footprints. The study also stated the critical challenges, such as the high energy demands of the aluminum PBF-LB/M process and its scalability limitations. Potential sustainable solutions were discussed starting from powder production techniques, as well as optimized processes and post-processing strategies. By adopting an interdisciplinary approach, this research highlighted the pivotal role of PBFed aluminum alloys in achieving sustainable manufacturing goals. It provided actionable insights to drive innovation and resilience in industrial applications, offering a roadmap for balancing environmental stewardship with the demands of high-performance standards. Additively manufactured (AM) aluminum (Al) alloys with high as-built ductility offer sustainability, enhanced load-bearing performance, and resistance to residual-stress-induced failure. However, most commercial AM Al alloys have very limited ductility. In this study, we designed an AM Al-1.63Zr-2.38Er-1.34Ni (wt. %) alloy with 16% as-built ductility, while not introducing nanopowders or expensive scandium (Sc) to the formulation. We revealed that Al3Zr accounted for 65% of cavitation in the as-built condition by SEM characterizations. With calculation of phase diagram (CALPHAD)-based integrated computational materials engineering (ICME) simulations, we found that at each Er composition, Zr must not exceed the threshold required to act as a reservoir for the L12 phase transformation (needed for high strength) during aging. An optimized composition was identified following the guideline of Zr = 1.07 × Er; this composition enhances the ductility from 0.9% to 16% (1600% increase) in the as-built sample, while only decreasing strength by 27% compared to the benchmark alloy. The strength is preserved even after aging for 48 hours at 400°C.

Abstract:
Additive manufacturing of aluminum (Al) alloys has attracted significant attention in the aerospace industry. However, achieving ultrahigh-strength (>500 MPa) Al alloys remains challenging due to their intrinsic poor printability. Here, we report a novel hybrid additive manufacturing (HAM) approach to process ultrahigh-strength AlMgSc alloy, which combines laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) with interlayer ultrasonic shot peening (USP). The results show that the interlayer ultrasonic shot peening depth reached ∼700 µm, leading to almost full density and residual stress convection from tension to compression. The HAM method promotes equiaxed grain formation and refines grain due to grain recrystallizations. Interestingly, the HAM followed by aging treatment tailors the hierarchically multi-gradient structures, inhibits Mg element intragranular segregation, and promotes the multi-nanoprecipitates (e.g. Al3(Sc, Zr) and Al6Mn) precipitation. Remarkably, the HAM followed by aging treatment achieves yield strength of 609 MPa and breaks elongation of 7.5%, demonstrating ultrahigh strength and good ductility compared with other Al alloys manufactured by AM and forging as reported in the literature. The strength enhancement mechanisms in this AlMgSc alloy are discussed. The high-density Al3(Sc, Zr) precipitates are the main strengthening contributor, and unique hetero-deformation induced (HDI) strengthening (originates from the heterogeneous microstructures) further enhances the strength of the material. This work highlights a novel approach for processing complex-structured ultrahigh strength Al alloy components by hybrid additive manufacturing.

                  <jats:p>Focusing on the problems of complicated sample processing and long detection time of traditional bauxite ore composition testing in mining areas, this paper proposes a rapid bauxite ore classification method combining cavity-confined laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (CC-LIBS) with Boruta feature selection and Bayesian optimization eXtreme Gradient Boosting (BBO-XGBoost), which can quickly and accurately classify bauxite ore samples from 9 different mining areas. First, the effects of different cavity configurations on the enhancement factor, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), were investigated. When the cavity diameter is 5 mm, the enhancement factors for Al, Fe, and Ti reach 2.8, 3.1, and 2.6, respectively. Next, 900 × 12,248-dimensional spectral data under the D = 5 mm cavity configuration were preprocessed using the Boruta feature selection algorithm. Finally, the XGBoost classifier is optimized using Bayesian optimization to achieve accurate classification of bauxite. Compared with unoptimized approaches and other models, the classification method combining CC-LIBS and BBO-XGBoost achieves the best performance. The accuracy is 0.9852, the precision is 0.9861, the recall is 0.9852, and the F1-score is 0.9856. The proposed technique, combining CC-LIBS with BBO-XGBoost, not only plays a pivotal role in bauxite ore research but also provides a significant technical reference for the rapid identification of bauxite ore sources.</jats:p>

Droplet jetting technologies offer a versatile, digital platform to fabricate functional devices from nanomaterial building blocks. Inkjet, aerosol jet, and electrohydrodynamic jet printing constitute three distinct technologies for precise patterning of functional materials in an additive, digital, and noncontact manner. While the unique physical mechanism of each technology endows it with specific advantages and disadvantages, commonalities in materials compatibility, patterning capabilities, and application domains motivate a holistic assessment of nanomaterial integration with these methods. This report will highlight progress across ink formulation, process design, and application development from recent years, with an emphasis on emerging materials and practical applications in this evolving field of research. This includes an overview of the three printing technologies, a survey of ink formulation and printing efforts across conductive, insulating, and semiconducting materials, an examination of compelling application demonstrations in electronics, sensing, and energy, as well as discussion of key emerging themes related to artificial intelligence, multimaterial printing, and nonplanar patterning.

Abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Metal halide perovskite photovoltaics have emerged as promising next-generation solar technologies owing to their high efficiency and compatibility with low-temperature manufacturing. Although small-area perovskite solar cells have achieved certified efficiencies around 28%, scalable fabrication of large-area perovskite films and modules remains a major challenge for commercialization. During scale-up, film formation becomes highly sensitive to coupled transport and solidification processes, including fluid flow, solvent evaporation, vapor transport, supersaturation evolution, nucleation, crystal growth, and phase conversion. These processes generate spatiotemporal heterogeneities that cause nonuniform crystallization, defect formation, and module-level performance losses. In this Review, we establish a crystallization-centered framework for understanding large-area perovskite film fabrication across both solution-based and vapor-based deposition routes. Solution processing methods are discussed from the perspectives of wet-film hydrodynamics and solvent-mediated crystallization, while vapor-based routes are analyzed in terms of precursor transport, surface reaction kinetics, and non-equilibrium growth. Previous studies are further used to relate precursor transport and perovskite crystallization control to film uniformity, device performance, and operational stability. Finally, we discuss emerging strategies for crystallization control and scalable manufacturing toward reliable, high-throughput perovskite photovoltaic modules.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Edible coatings are widely studied as food-compatible formulations for reducing moisture loss, oxidation, microbial spoilage, oil uptake, and quality deterioration. Their translation from laboratory formulation to industrial use, however, depends not only on film-forming composition but also on controlled deposition, retained dose, surface coverage, drying history, defect formation, hygienic operation, and reproducible performance on heterogeneous food surfaces. An OpenAlex-supported evidence-map audit (2014–2026) was used to separate direct food-coating validation from adjacent engineering models. This review reframes edible coatings as engineered deposited interfaces and proposes a claim-controlled, evidence-tiered framework linking food-grade biopolymer fluids, processability, atomization, droplet impact, wet-film evolution, dry-film structure, image-based metrology, multiphase modeling, and food-performance endpoints. This review outlines the prerequisites for future digital-twin-ready edible coating workflows by linking functional biopolymer fluids, deposition technologies, droplet physics, intelligent image metrology, Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD), Volume of Fluid (VOF), uncertainty reporting, food-performance endpoints, safety, Life-Cycle Assessment (LCA), Techno-Economic Analysis (TEA) and patent-aware innovation. Digital twins are treated as a future integration target that depends on validated inputs, standardized reporting, deposition metrology and food-specific model validation. The central argument is that progress in edible coatings requires fewer isolated formulation claims and stronger validated links between deposited-interface properties and food-relevant function. A minimum reporting checklist is proposed to support reproducible comparison of deposition routes, coating structures, and translation potential.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Superhydrophobic coatings have been applied in various fields. The materials used in the preparation of superhydrophobic coatings have attracted the attention of scholars. Due to the harm of fluorine-containing substances with low surface energy to the environment, fluorine-free superhydrophobic coatings have become a hotspot in the research field. Herein, a fluorine-free superhydrophobic coating with oil/water separation was made by a solution immersion way. The fluorine-free copolymer and polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS)/SiO2 nanoparticles (NPs) were mixed to prepare a composite solution, and the superhydrophobic surface was obtained on the paper by a dipping method. The scanning electron microscope, x-ray photoelectron spectrometer, 1H nuclear magnetic resonance, and Fourier transform infrared were used to study the surface characteristics and structural composition of the superhydrophobic material. The research proved that the copolymer and PDMS/SiO2 NPs were successfully coated on the paper surface, and the rough structure of the superhydrophobic surface was also attributed to the introduction of the copolymer and PDMS/SiO2 NPs. The evaluation of the coating has proved its excellent hydrophobicity, oil/water separation performance, and self-cleaning performance. The coating is a sustainable and environmentally friendly superhydrophobic material that can be used in packaging, construction, petrochemical, and other industries.

## 1. ekaputra2026coarseningandcreepbehavior pages 1-4 (Context ID: pqac-00000003)

               Coarsening- and creep behavior of supersaturated Al-Zr-X
         (X = Mn, Cr, V, Mo, W) alloys processed by laser powder-bed fusion

     Clement N. Ekaputraa, Ekin Senvardarlia, Christian Leinenbachb,c, David C. Dunanda

         a Department of Materials Science and Engineering, Northwestern University, Evanston, IL 60208, USA

        b Empa, Swiss Federal Laboratories for Materials Science and Technology, Dübendorf 8600, Switzerland

                 c École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), Laboratory for Photonic Materials and
                                   Characterization, Lausanne 1015, Switzerland


Abstract

We characterize the high-temperature microstructural evolution and creep properties of binary
Al-0.4Zr and ternary Al-0.4Zr-1X (at.%) alloys fabricated by laser-powder bed fusion (L-PBF),
where X = Mn, Cr, V, Mo, and W are slow-diffusing transition metals added for solid-solution
strengthening. All alloys contain strengthening L12-Al3Zr nanoprecipitates which form during
aging at 400°C. In the as-fabricated alloys, the ternary solute is nearly all in solid solution in the
Mn- and Cr-containing alloys, and partially in solution in the V-, Mo-, and W-containing alloys,
but still in amounts well beyond the equilibrium solubility limit for these elements. Solid
solutions of the ternary solutes decompose during long-term aging at 400°C to form binary Al-X
precipitates. The relative rates of precipitation of these elements are consistent with their relative
diffusivities in Al: the precipitation rate is fastest for Mn, followed by Cr, then V, Mo, and W
(the latter three elements remain almost entirely in solid solution after 2016 h exposure at
400°C). Nevertheless, the strengthening contribution from the ternary solute at room temperature
does not significantly differ among the five studied alloys or as a function of aging time at
400°C, indicating a stable strengthening contribution from Mn, Cr, V, Mo, and W in Al. During
creep deformation at 400°C, all ternary alloys show significantly higher creep resistance than a
binary Al-Zr alloy. Furthermore, their creep resistance is comparable to those of additively-
manufactured alloys with significantly higher volume fractions of strengthening phases.1. Introduction

Aluminum-based alloys processed by laser powder-bed fusion (L-PBF) additive manufacturing
often have unique, non-equilibrium microstructures due to the fast cooling rates (>105-106 K/s)
inherent to the L-PBF process [1]. One important aspect of these non-equilibrium
microstructures is the ability to achieve extended solid solutions well beyond their maximum
equilibrium solubility [2]. As a result, Al-based alloys designed for additive manufacturing can
be more heavily alloyed than those designed for conventional, near-equilibrium solidification
(such as casting), and by extension often display much enhanced mechanical properties due to
greater solid-solution or secondary-precipitation strengthening [1].

One important example of such alloys are L12-strengthened Al alloys, where high amounts of
L12-forming elements (Sc, Zr, Ti) beyond their maximum solid solubilities in Al promote both
printability and large strengthening responses during secondary aging [3, 4]. Two prominent
commercial examples of such alloys are Al-Mg-Sc-Zr (Scalmalloy) [5] and Al-Mg-Zr
(Addalloy) [6] alloys, but many similar alloys exist in the literature (e.g., Al-Mn-Mg-Sc-Zr [7],
Al-Mn-Cr-Zr [8], Al-Cu-Mn-Zr [9], Al-Cu-Sc-Zr [10], Al-Zn-Mg-Sc-Zr [11]), where high
amounts of additional alloying elements (Mg, Mn, Cu, Cr, Zn) beyond their equilibrium
solubility limits provide additional solid-solution or precipitation strengthening. In this work, we
focus on the high-temperature solid-solution strengthening effect of five transition metals in
ternary Al-Zr-X systems, for design of Al alloys with excellent high-temperature mechanical
properties.

Here, we study the addition of Mn, Cr, V, Mo, and W to the Al-Zr system. Among the various
solid-solution strengthening elements in Al, these five elements provide some of the highest
solid-solution strengthening increments per at.% added [1, 12]. This is due to their large lattice
misfit in Al: from first-principles calculations [12], a 75-125 MPa yield-strength increment can
be expected from 1 at.% addition of these elements, as opposed to <25 MPa/at.% from Mg or Zn.
However, the low equilibrium solid solubility of these elements in Al limits the amount that can
be added under conventional processes, but the rapid solidification rates provided by L-PBF AM
enables much higher amounts of these elements to be added in supersaturated solid solution,
increasing their possible solution strengthening effect. For example, Al-4.5Mn-1.3Mg-0.79Sc-
0.74Zr (wt.%) [13] and Al-5.0Mn-0.8Cr-0.6Zr (wt.%) [8] alloys processed by L-PBF fully retain
their respective amounts of Mn and Cr in solid solution after L-PBF, leading to high strength in
the as-fabricated state. Earlier work in the rapid solidification literature on the binary Al-Mn, Al-
Cr, Al-V, Al-Mo, and Al-W systems [14] suggests that 2.2% Mn, 0.94% Cr, 0.53% V, 0.18%
Mo, and 0.18% W (at.%), respectively, is retained in solid solution for cooling rates of 103-104
K/s. Similar studies show as much as 2.0 at.% V [15], 2.45 at.% Mo [16], and 1.0 at.% W [17]
can be obtained for higher cooling rates (>105 K/s), which are more similar to the cooling rates
expected in L-PBF [1], suggesting high amounts of possible solid-solution strengthening from
alloys containing these elements.

Furthermore, previous experimental work indicates that slow-diffusing solute elements can also
provide resistance to creep deformation at high temperatures. The creep strengthening effect of
Mn solutes have been widely studied. In a study by Farkoosh et al. [18], the presence of just 0.5at.% Mn in an Al-0.5Mn-0.02Si alloy reduced creep strain rates at 300°C by 5-6 orders of
magnitude when compared to pure Al. In the same study, the dislocation creep threshold stress of
an Al-0.5Mn-0.09Zr-0.05Er-0.05Si alloy was more than three times higher than that of a similar
Al-0.11Zr-0.005Er (at.%) alloy without Mn. Similar results have been found in cast Al-Ce-Mn
[19] and L-PBF processed Al-Mn-Sc [20] alloys. In all these studies, it is proposed that attractive
forces exerted by slow-diffusing Mn atoms slow the climb of dislocations, reducing creep strain
rates. More generally, other slow-diffusing elements, such as Fe [21], also improve creep
resistance, while fast-diffusing elements such as Cu, Zn, and Bi [22] provide no creep
strengthening and may even increase creep strain rates.

A natural question, then, is whether solutes which diffuse even slower than Mn in Al – such as
Cr, V, Mo, and W – also have a stronger creep strengthening effect than Mn when in solid
solution in Al. The diffusivity of Mn at 400 °C is 9 x 10-19 m2/s, that of Cr is two orders of
magnitude lower (1.3 x 10-21 m2/s), and those of V, Mo, and W are 5-6 orders of magnitude
lower than Mn (5 x 10-24, 5 x 10-23, and 5 x 10-23 m2/s, respectively) [23]. Several previous
studies have examined the effects of slow diffusing elements (Cr, V, Mo, W) on the creep
resistance of Zr-containing cast Al alloys [24-28], but only in small amounts (<0.1 at.%) as the
achievable solubility of these elements in cast alloys is quite low. Earlier studies have reported
improved creep rupture life in more concentrated, rapidly-solidified, binary Al-Cr, -V, -Mo, or -
W alloys [14], but do not report the secondary creep strain rates in these alloys. Thus, there is a
gap in the literature on the creep properties of rapidly-solidified Al alloys strengthened by stable,
extended solid solutions.

Here, we study six L-PBF processed Al alloys: a binary Al-0.4Zr alloy, and five ternary Al-
0.4Zr-1X (at.%) alloys, where X = Mn, Cr, V, Mo, or W are all slow-diffusing transition metal
elements. The 1 at.% concentration of the ternary solute is selected based on the above literature
suggesting that this amount could be retained in solid solution for rapidly-solidified binary Al-X
alloys, and kept constant between alloys to isolate effects of the solute itself on microstructure
and mechanical properties. We focus first on the as-fabricated, rapidly-solidified microstructure
of these alloys to determine if supersaturated solid solutions of these elements can be achieved.
Then, we evaluate the stability of these solid solutions during aging at temperatures >400°C, and
the effect of any precipitation on the room-temperature microhardness. Lastly, we study the
effect of these alloying elements on compressive creep properties at 400°C, comparing the effect
of alloying element and aging condition.2. Experimental procedures

Six alloy compositions were prepared: a binary Al-0.4Zr (at.%) alloy, and five ternary Al-0.4Zr-
1X (at.%) alloys, where X = Mn, Cr, V, Mo, or W. For brevity, these alloys will be referred to as
Al-Zr and Al-Zr-X alloys. Binary master alloys (Al-20Zr, Al-18.45Mn, Al-10Cr, Al-10V, Al-
20Mo, and Al-30W, wt.%) and high-purity Al (99.99%) were used as starting materials. The
binary Al-Cr, Al-V, Al-Mo, and Al-W master alloys were previously arc-melted from pure
starting elements in a Ti-gettered, purified argon atmosphere, and re-melted and flipped at least 8
times to ensure homogeneity. The master alloys were then combined and arc-melted into rods in
a rod-shaped copper hearth on a rePOWDER Ultrasonic Powder Atomizer (AMAZEMET), also
under Ti-gettered, argon atmosphere. The surface of the rods was ground off to increase
cleanliness. The rods were then atomized on the same instrument, using a water-cooled
molybdenum (TZM) sonotrode vibrating at 40 kHz and plasma torch with a melting current of
~220 A under Ar atmosphere (<50 ppm O2). The resulting powder was sieved to 20-100 µm,
also under Ar atmosphere.

The powders were fused on a Sisma MYSINT100 SLM printer (1070 nm Yb fiber laser). A
parameter study was first conducted, using constant 200 W laser power, 30 µm powder layer
thickness, 100 µm hatch spacing, 55 µm spot size, and bidirectional scan strategy, and the scan
speed was either 200, 400, 600, 800, or 1000 mm/s. Two cubes (5x5x5 mm) were printed per
parameter set for each alloy. The cubes were then cross-sectioned and polished, and defects were
observed qualitatively via optical microscopy (Zeiss Axiovert 100A). An appropriate parameter
set which yielded low amounts of printing defects for all alloy compositions (scan speed 800
mm/s) was determined and then used to print larger rectangular specimens (25 x 15 x 12 mm)
used for further microstructural and mechanical property analyses. The same parameter set was
used for all alloy compositions to isolate the effects of alloy composition from processing
parameters; it can be seen in Fig. S1 (Supplementary Information) that few defects were obtained
under these processing conditions in all alloys.

For microstructural characterization, the alloys were sectioned such that the XZ or YZ planes
(where Z is the build direction) of the specimens could be observed. For SEM and EDS analyses,
specimens were mounted, then prepared by mechanical grinding and polishing using SiC papers
(320, 600, 800, 1200 grit), water-based diamond slurry (6, then 3 µm), and colloidal silica (0.06
µm) suspension. The final polishing step was vibratory polishing for ~20 min using 0.06 µm
colloidal silica suspension. For EBSD analyses, the specimens were de-mounted, then attached
to an SEM stub and subjected to further vibratory polishing (~4 h) to further improve surface
quality. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) was performed on a JEOL 7900F SEM with an
Oxford detector for energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) measurements. Electron
backscatter diffraction (EBSD) was performed on an FEI Quanta 650 SEM with an Oxford
EBSD system, using a scanning area of 524 x 360 µm and step size of 1 µm. X-ray diffraction
(XRD) analyses were obtained on the polished surfaces, using a Rigaku Smartlab 3 kW
instrument in reflection geometry, with a Cu source operating at 40 kV and 35 mA. Atom probe
tomography (non-site-specific) was performed using a LEAP 5000 XS tomograph. To prepare
the specimen tips, 0.3 x 0.3 x ~10 mm rectangular blanks were prepared by cutting with aprecision saw, which were then electropolished using a two-step procedure. The blanks were first
thinned to create a neck using a solution of 10% perchloric acid in acetic acid, using a voltage of
12-25 VDC; the neck was then further thinned and the tip was separated using a solution of 2%
perchloric acid in butoxyethanol, using a voltage of 3-12 VDC. APT data were collected at 30 K,
using a 30 pJ pulse and frequency of 500 kHz. The tomographic datasets were then reconstructed
using IVAS 3.8.16, the mass spectra were background-corrected, and the proximity histogram
(proxigram) method was used to analyze the tips.

The LPBF Al-Zr-X specimens were subjected to a peak-aging treatment at 400°C, then further
overaging either for up to three months at 400°C or for 24 h at 590°C. Samples were taken out of
the furnace after various times for microhardness and electrical conductivity measurements, or
microstructural observation as detailed earlier. Microhardness testing was performed using a
Wilson VH3100 automated microhardness tester, making 20 indents per sample using a 200 g
load and 5 s dwell time. Regions with obvious porosity or inclusions were avoided. Electrical
conductivity was measured on a ~1 mm thick sample using a Sigmatest 2.069 eddy current
instrument (Foerster Instruments). The sample surface was cleaned with ethanol prior to
measurement. Five measurements were made each at 240, 480, and 960 Hz per test condition for
a total of 15 measurements, which were then averaged.

Compressive creep was performed on all Al-Zr-X alloys. Creep specimens with square cross
section (~ 5 x 5 x 10 mm) were sectioned from the printed blocks, and the top and bottom of the
creep specimens were carefully ground to be flat and parallel. The loading direction was parallel
to the build direction. The creep specimens were then held at 400°C for 4 h (peak-aging) or 504
h (over aging) prior to creep. The specimens were placed between two tungsten carbide
compression platens which had been lubricated with boron nitride, and inserted in a compressive
creep cage. Creep testing was performed under air atmosphere at 400°C (±1°C), where the
temperature was verified by an external thermocouple in contact with the sample. Load was
applied via a lever-arm with hanging dead weights, and strain was measured via a linear voltage
displacement transducer (LVDT). After soaking for at least 1 h at the test temperature, a constant
load was applied and the strain was measured, until a steady-state strain rate was achieved. At
that point, the load was increased, and this process was repeated until a total strain of ~10% was
accumulated in the sample. The total creep time for each sample tested in this way was between
90 and 144h.3. Results

3.3.1. Microhardness evolution

The microhardness evolution of the binary Al-Zr and Al-Zr-X alloys during aging at 400°C is
shown in Fig. 7. The microhardness of the as-LPBF binary Al-Zr alloy is 441 ± 20 MPa and
increases by ~500 MPa during initial aging at 400°C. The hardness increases up to a plateau
which lasts from 4 to 24 h aging time. The peak-aging time at 400°C was chosen as 4 h (marked
by vertical dashed line). After the hardness plateau, the microhardness decreases slowly to 722 ±
50 MPa after three months of overaging at 400°C. This aging behavior is consistent with
precipitation of nano-scale L12-Al3Zr precipitates during initial stages of aging (as observed in
Section 3.2), strengthening the alloy. These precipitates then coarsen during over-aging, resulting
in loss of strength which is accelerated at higher temperatures. The ternary Al-Zr-X alloys
exhibit the same hardness trend as the binary Al-Zr alloy, but their hardness is ~200 MPa higher
than that of the Al-Zr alloys at all stages of aging. The as-LPBF hardness ranges from 577-716
MPa ,and increases to 1150-1250 MPa during peak-aging at 400°C, then decreases slowly to
860-1013 MPa during overaging at 400°C. Among the five ternary Al-Zr-X alloys, the hardness
does not vary substantially between alloy compositions.

up to 2016 h or at 590°C for 24 h. The electrical conductivity scales inversely with solute
concentration in the matrix; furthermore, the contributions of solutes to decreasing electrical
conductivity significantly outweigh those from other lattice defects (e.g. precipitates,

mostly controlled by the precipitation of solute from solution. The electrical conductivity of the
binary Al-Zr alloy gradually increases during aging at 400°C (and faster at 590°C), consistent

the as-fabricated ternary Al-Zr-X alloys is lower than that of the binary Al-Zr alloy, due to the
ternary solute elements in solid solution which further contribute to electron scattering.
Furthermore, the electrical conductivity of all ternary alloys increases during aging, indicative of
Zr and/or the ternary solute precipitating from solid solution, which form as binary Al-Zr or Al-
X precipitates (identified later in Section 3.3.3).

BSE-SEM micrographs of the Al-Zr and Al-Zr-X alloys during aging are provided in Fig. 9, in
three different aging conditions: mild over-aging (400°C/8h, within the 4-24h hardness plateau,
Fig. 9(a1-f1)), over-aging (400°C/1008h (Fig. 9(a2-f2)), and extreme over-aging (590°C/24h
(Fig. 9(a3-f3)).

In the mildly-overaged (400°C/8h) state, some equiaxed precipitates (with bright contrast) are
visible in the binary Al-Zr alloy (Fig. 9(a1)). These may be either primary L12 precipitates which
were not visible in the as-fabricated state and coarsened during aging, or relatively coarse
secondary L12 precipitates forming exclusively during aging. In the Al-Zr-Mn alloy (Fig. 9(b1)),
micron-scale, platelike precipitates are visible; some coarser precipitates also appear which are
indicated with yellow arrows. Within the grains, submicron, plate-like precipitates are visible.
The Al-Zr-Cr alloy (Fig. 9(c1)) also shows some micron-scale, plate-like precipitates at grain
boundaries and submicron precipitates within the grains, but both the size and number density of
these precipitates are smaller than those of the Al-Zr-Mn alloy. In the Al-Zr-V (Fig. 9(d1)), -Mo
(Fig. 9(e1)), and -W (Fig. 9(f1)) alloys, precipitates at grain boundaries are visible, but not within
the grains, and these precipitates are smaller and fewer in number than those in the Al-Zr-Cr
alloy. In all alloys, regions of darker contrast are visible immediately around the precipitates,
both within the grains and at grain boundaries, which may indicate local depletion of solute due
to formation of grain boundary precipitates.

After overaging for 1008 h at 400°C, rounder, light-contrast precipitates are visible in the binary
Al-Zr alloy (Fig. 9(a2)), indicating further coarsening of the L12-Al3Zr precipitates. Some larger
precipitates are visible at grain boundaries, consistent with transformation of L12-Al3Zr (which
takes on equiaxed morphologies) to D023-Al3Zr which occurs at longer aging times and takes on
a rod-like morphology [33]. The Al-Zr-Mn (Fig. 9(b2)) and Al-Zr-Cr (Fig. 9(c2)) alloys again
contain precipitates at both grain boundaries and grain interiors, and these precipitates are
significantly coarser than they were after 8h of aging in their respective alloys, with those in the
Al-Zr-Cr alloy being less numerous and smaller than those in the Al-Zr-Mn alloy. The Al-Zr-V
(Fig. 9(d2)), -Mo (Fig. 9(e2)), and -W (Fig. 9(f2)) alloys contain precipitates at grain boundaries
which are again coarser than after 8h at 400°C, with no visible intragranular precipitates.

treatment (Supplementary Information, Fig. S4) identify these phases as Al12Mn, Al7Cr, Al21V2,
Al12Mo, and Al12W, respectively, consistent with previous studies in these binary Al-X systems
[31, 34-37].

During extreme over-aging at 590°C for 24h, the binary Al-Zr alloy (Fig. 9(a3)) contains many
precipitates with an elongated morphology, consistent with the transformation of Al3Zr from the
L12 to the D023 crystal structure. XRD analyses (Supplementary Information, Fig. S4) of the
binary Al-Zr (and all ternary Al-Zr-X alloys) after this aging treatment indicate the presence of
D023-Al3Zr. In the ternary alloys (Fig. 9(b3-f3)), precipitates are visible in all alloys in both the
grain interiors and grain boundaries. These precipitates are coarsest in the Al-Zr-Mn alloy (>1
µm), finer in the Al-Zr-Cr alloy (~1 µm), and finest in the Al-Zr-V, -Mo, and -W alloys(submicron). XRD analyses (Fig. S4) again identify these precipitates as Al12Mn, Al7Cr, Al21V2,
Al12Mo, and Al12W, respectively.

precipitation of their ternary solutes (and stability of solid solutions) differs among alloys. At
400°C, significant intragranular precipitation of the ternary solute occurs only for the Al-Zr-Mn
and Al-Zr-Cr alloys, slower in the latter alloy. No intragranular precipitation is observed at
400°C via SEM in either the Al-Zr-V, -Mo, or -W alloys, but precipitates formed at 590°C.
Grain-boundary precipitates were observed in all alloys, even at 400°C.Figure 9. BSE-SEM micrographs during aging of the (a) binary Al-Zr, and ternary (b) Al-Zr-Mn, (c) -Cr, (d) -V, (e)
-Mo, and (f) -W alloys. (a1-f1) show micrographs for a mild over-aging treatment (400°C/8h), (a2-f2) for severe
over-aging (400°C/1008h), and (a3-f3) for extreme over-aging (590°C/24h). Yellow arrows point to coarser

Compressive creep experiments were performed at 400°C on the Al-Zr and ternary Al-Zr-X
alloys in both peak-aged (400C/4h) and over-aged (400C/504h) conditions; results are shown
double-logarithmic plots of the minimum creep strain rates vs. applied stress in Fig. 10. All
alloys show two creep regimes, one at low stresses with a low stress exponent (n ~ 1-2)
characteristic of diffusional creep, and one at high stresses with a high apparent creep stress
exponent (napp ~ 8-11) characteristic of dislocation creep. The dislocation creep regime is
typically modeled by a power law, 𝜀̇ = 𝐴𝜎𝑛𝑎𝑝𝑝, where 𝜀̇ is the minimum secondary creep strain
rate, A is a temperature-dependent constant, 𝜎 is the applied stress, and 𝑛𝑎𝑝𝑝 is the apparent
stress exponent. The apparent creep stress exponent in the dislocation creep regime is much
higher than the matrix stress exponent for Al (n ~ 4.4), typical of precipitation-strengthened
alloys and indicative of a threshold stress, σth, below which moving dislocations are stopped by
the L12-Al3Zr nanoprecipitates and dislocation creep is inhibited [38]. The power law can be
expressed accounting for the threshold stress as 𝜀̇ = 𝐴′(𝜎−𝜎𝑡ℎ)𝑛, where A’ is a new constant
and n is the matrix stress exponent. The threshold stress can be determined by a best-fit
procedure as in Refs. [39, 40], and threshold stresses for all alloys tested in this study are
visualized in Fig. 10 (error bars estimated as ±1 MPa), and exact values are listed in
Supplementary Information (Table S2).

Comparing the peak-aged binary Al-Zr and ternary Al-Zr-X alloys (Fig. 10(a)), all ternary Al-Zr-
X alloys are significantly more creep-resistant than the binary Al-Zr alloy. The creep strain rates
in the ternary Al-Zr-X alloys are 2-3 orders of magnitude lower for fixed stress; also, the
dislocation creep threshold stresses are 2-3x higher than that of the binary Al-Zr alloy (Table 3,
Fig. 10(c)). Creep strain rates in the Al-Zr-Mo and -W alloys are 1-2 orders of magnitude lower
than that of the Al-Zr-Mn, -Cr, and -V alloys, and their threshold stresses for dislocation creep
are also higher by ~10 MPa. The hardness of the peak-aged alloys after creep testing (Fig. S5,
Supplementary Information) has slightly decreased, likely due to the long duration of the creep

## 1. taheri‐mousavi2026additivelymanufacturablehigh‐strength pages 1-4 (Context ID: pqac-00000008)

  Additively manufacturable high-strength aluminum alloys with thermally stable

        microstructures enabled by hybrid machine learning-based design


         S. Mohadeseh Taheri-Mousavi1,2,3,4*, Michael Xu2, Florian Hengsbach5, Clay Houser2,6,

 Zhaoxuan Ge3, Benjamin Glaser3, Shaolou Wei2, Mirko Schaper5, James M. LeBeau2, Greg B.

                                   Olson2, A. John Hart1*


         1Department of Mechanical Engineering, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, 77
                   Massachusetts Avenue, Cambridge, MA 02139, USA.
 2Department of Materials Science and Engineering, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, 77
                   Massachusetts Avenue, Cambridge, MA 02139, USA.
  3Department of Materials Science and Engineering, Carnegie Mellon University, 5000 Forbes
                         Avenue, Pittsburgh, PA 15213, USA.
  4Department of Mechanical Engineering, Carnegie Mellon University, 5000 Forbes Avenue,
                                   Pittsburgh, PA 15213, USA.
5Department of Mechanical Engineering, Paderborn University, Mersinweg 9, 33100 Paderborn,
                                 Germany
   6Department of Materials Science and Engineering, Northwestern University, Evanston, IL
                                     60208, USA

               *Corresponding authors: smtaherimousavi@cmu.edu; ajhart@mit.edu


Summary paragraph

       Additively manufactured (AM) aluminum alloys with high strength and thermal stability

have broad applications in turbine engines, vacuum pumps, heat exchangers, and many other

industrial systems. Employing precipitates with an L12 structure to block dislocation motions is a

widespread strategy to strengthen aluminum. However, to achieve high strength, a high volume

fraction of small precipitates is required, and these characteristics are generally mutually exclusive.

Here, we show that for certain compositions of Al alloys, L12 phases initially precipitate as sub-

micron metastable ternary phases under the rapid solidification conditions of powder bed AM, yet

the subsequent L12 phases that precipitate during heat treatment of the sample remain at the

nanoscale, imparting high strength. For strength to be retained at elevated temperature, these

nanoprecipitates must have low coarsening rates. To inversely design the composition of an alloy

to have these target microstructural features, we used hybrid calculation of phase diagram

(CALPHAD)-based  integrated  computational  materials  engineering (ICME) and Bayesian



                                                                                    1optimization techniques. We tested our approach by designing an Al-Er-Zr-Y-Yb-Ni model alloy,

and the selected composition was manufactured in powder form as AM feedstock. The strength of

specimens manufactured via laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) from the designed composition is

comparable to that of wrought Al 7075, yet without cracking that occurs upon LPBF of Al 7075.
After high-temperature (400°C) aging the designed alloy is 50% stronger than the strongest known

benchmark printable Al alloy1. This stable strengthening strategy is applicable to a wide range of

alloys and rapid solidification processes, and our hybrid ML/CALPHAD numerical framework

can be used for the efficient and robust design of alloy microstructures and properties, expanding

the capabilities of additive as well as traditional manufacturing.

Introduction

       Additively manufactured (AM) structural components with complex geometries and

tailored properties at voxel-size resolution will lead to significant leap in performance in various

critical engineering applications. One of the exceptional benefits of AM is that exploiting non-

equilibrium processing pathways, including through  rapid  solidification, can give  rise  to

precipitation of metastable phases1–4, supersaturation of solutes5–7, refining length scales of

microstructural features such as grain and phase size8–13. These microstructural features are

difficult or impossible to develop in slow solidification conditions such as during casting. For

example, metastable phases due to rapid solidification have been reported in Ni, Fe, Ti, Al alloys

and alter their mechanical properties or printability at different length scales2,3,14–20. The features

may also appear in welding, giga casting, and splat quenching when the processing conditions lead

to rapid solidification. Exploiting the rapid solidification may thus unravel new routes for alloy

design.

      Al alloys are the second widest used alloys after steels in industrial applications21. High

(temperature)  strength Al  alloys have been mainly  strengthened with two mechanisms8.

Employing precipitates especially with L12 structures is the first main strategy22. L12 structures

are preferred due to having coherent interfaces to resist coarsening at high temperatures. As the

second strategy, Al grains can be partitioned with eutectic phases to further block dislocation

motions 8. Following the first strategy, strength has an inverse relationship with the precipitate size

based on the Orowan strengthening theory22. Thus, for a given volume fraction of precipitates,

smaller precipitate sizes more effectively block dislocation motions and lead to higher strength.



                                                                                    2Although laser AM processing generally leads to smaller length scales as phases do not have time
