Abstract

Refractory multi-principal element alloys offer high melting temperatures and
compositional flexibility for structural applications under extreme conditions. In the
Nb–Ti–Zr ternary system, Zr confers corrosion resistance and a low neutron capture
cross-section, while Nb stabilizes the body-centered cubic (BCC) phase across a
wide composition space, and Ti, the lightest constituent, lowers the alloy density.
Here we report the first additive manufacturing of Nb25Ti20Zr55 by laser powder bed
fusion (LPBF) and laser directed energy deposition (LDED) from a single prealloyed
powder. Both routes produced intact builds with sparse pores across much of the
processing window, with cracking confined to part of the LPBF range. Electron         Pre-proof
backscatter diffraction and X-ray diffraction indexed a predominantly body-centered
cubic microstructure at Zr contents of 50.4 to 55.5 at.% across both routes. Ti
evaporated preferentially, falling 9.5 at.% from the feedstock in LPBF, yet the BCC
phase was retained. The LPBF composition was uniform across the processing
window. The LDED composition varied with energy density and approached the
LPBF value only at the highest energy density. LPBF gave finer grains (96 µm) than
LDED (140 µm) at equivalent hardness (H = 2.73 to 2.90 GPa) and Young’s modulus
(E = 79 to 83 GPa).   Journal

1  Introduction
Refractory metals and their alloys are attractive candidates for high-temperature
structural applications because of their high melting temperatures and their ability to
retain strength at temperatures exceeding the service limits of nickel-based
superalloys [1]. Among the refractory elements, Zr offers good corrosion resistance,
and a low thermal neutron capture cross-section, making Zr-based alloys the
standard cladding material in light water reactors [2], [3]. Despite decades of
development, broader deployment of refractory alloys has been constrained by
manufacturing difficulty: the high processing temperatures, limited room-temperature
ductility, and strong oxygen affinity of these materials impose severe constraints on
conventional fabrication routes [1]. For Zr-rich refractory alloy design,
multicomponent alloying provides a route to preserve the Zr-centered design
rationale while modifying phase stability and processability.



1Refractory multi-principal element alloys (RMPEAs) expand the accessible
compositional space by distributing multiple refractory elements in non-equiatomic
proportions, enabling independent alteration of phase stability, density, and
mechanical properties beyond the limits of conventional single-principal-element
refractory alloys [1].The Nb–Ti–Zr ternary system is particularly attractive because
Nb, Ti, and Zr exhibit extensive mutual solubility in the body-centered cubic (BCC)
phase at elevated temperatures, providing a broad non-equiatomic composition
space at comparatively low density [4], [5]. Although Nb is BCC at all temperatures,
Ti and Zr are hexagonal close-packed (HCP) at room temperature and transform to
BCC only above ≈882 °C and ≈863 °C, respectively [6], [7]. The BCC phase can
nevertheless be retained across selected ternary compositions through Nb additions,
which act as a BCC stabilizer [4], and through rapid solidification, which can suppress
equilibrium phase decomposition. Recent high-throughput screening by Lech et al.
using magnetron-sputtered thin films mapped this ternary space and established that
single-phase BCC stability requires Zr contents below 30.5 at.%, with oxygen acting
as a critical destabilizing factor [4]. The nominal composition Nb25Ti20Zr55,
investigated here, contains 55 at.% Zr and therefore lies outside the predicted single-
phase BCC stability field. In our previous work [8], the same composition formed
BCC after annealing and was identified as a promising candidate for laser-based
manufacturing, where single-track experiments demonstrated laser–material
compatibility. However, the transition from single-track screening to bulk additive
manufacturing (AM) has not yet been reported.

AM, and specifically laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), is attractive for refractory alloys
because it enables near-net-shape fabrication directly from powder feedstock whileimposing rapid solidification that canPre-proofreduce segregation length scales [9], [10].
However, LPBF of refractory systems remains challenging: large thermal gradients
generate residual stresses that promote cracking [11], and defects may arise from
solidification-related phenomena or from solid-state thermal cracking during
subsequent cooling [10], [11], [12]. The resulting defect populations are highly
system specific. Mooraj et al. demonstrated nearly defect-free LPBF of near-
equiatomic TiZrNbTa via in situ alloying of elemental powders and use of a
normalized processing diagram to identify a suitable processing window [13]. Other
refractory compositions, however, remain highly susceptible to cracking even after   Journal
parameter optimization [10], [14], confirming that processability is alloy specific.
Conventional refractory alloys such as C103 (Nb–10Hf–1Ti) have been processed by
LPBF to near-full density [15], yet no commercial end-product made of a refractory
high-entropy alloy has been reported to date [16]. Laser directed energy deposition
(LDED) provides a complementary additive route. Compared with LPBF, LDED
operates at lower cooling rates, larger melt pools, and lower spatial resolution, and it
accommodates feedstock variability through controlled powder flow into the melt pool
[9], [17], [18], [19]. Keyhole porosity and balling are melt pool instabilities associated
with the high beam intensities and scan speeds typical of LPBF [9], [18], whereas
LDED is more susceptible to dilution and macro-segregation [18]. LPBF and LDED
impose different cooling rat

operates at lower cooling rates, larger melt pools, and lower spatial resolution, and it
accommodates feedstock variability through controlled powder flow into the melt pool
[9], [17], [18], [19]. Keyhole porosity and balling are melt pool instabilities associated
with the high beam intensities and scan speeds typical of LPBF [9], [18], whereas
LDED is more susceptible to dilution and macro-segregation [18]. LPBF and LDED
impose different cooling rates, melt pool geometries, and mass transfer conditions.
The two routes may therefore produce different composition retention and
microstructural responses for the same alloy. Laser cladding of NbTiZr coatings on Zr
substrates has been reported [20], and LDED has been demonstrated for the related
quinary TiZrNbHfTa system [21]. However, bulk consolidation of the ternary Nb–Ti–Zr
alloy from the same prealloyed powder by both LPBF and LDED has not been
reported.


2Suitable powder feedstock is a further prerequisite for reliable laser-based AM. In
LPBF, powder spreading and recoating govern layer formation, whereas in LDED,
stable powder delivery and carrier gas transport govern material feeding into the melt
pool. Both routes therefore require chemically homogeneous powder with suitable
particle size distribution (PSD), morphology, and flowability [9], [16]. For
multicomponent refractory alloys, prealloyed powder is preferable when comparing
process routes because incomplete in situ alloying and local compositional
heterogeneity in blended elemental feedstock can obscure composition retention,
phase retention, and visible cracking responses [1], [13]. Using one prealloyed
powder for both LPBF and LDED minimizes feedstock variability, so that differences
between routes can be interpreted primarily in terms of processing conditions.
Ultrasonic atomization is well suited for this purpose because it produces spherical,
satellite-free powder with a controllable PSD [22]. Ultrasonically atomized metal
powder has been reported to exhibit good flowability [23], supporting its relevance for
powder spreading in LPBF and powder feeding in LDED [9], [16].

The present work investigates the AM of nominal Nb25Ti20Zr55 using two
complementary laser-based routes: LPBF and LDED. Prealloyed powder produced
by ultrasonic atomization was characterized for morphology, chemistry, and particle
size distribution, then used as feedstock for parametric processing trials in both LPBF
and LDED. Laser power and scan speed were varied at constant hatch spacing and
layer thickness for each process, and the resulting builds were assessed in
representative conditions for geometric integrity, visible cracking, composition
retention, phase constitution, and grain structure. Modified volumetric energy density
is used as a comparative descriptor to organize the LPBF and LDED parameterspaces. The study evaluates how processPre-proofroute affects composition retention, phase
constitution, and grain structure in a Zr-rich RMPEA processed from the same
prealloyed powder.

2.3  Microstructural characterization
Powder, LPBF, and LDED specimens were embedded in epoxy, ground with SiC
paper to 1000 grit, polished with 3 µm diamond suspension, and finished with 20 nm
colloidal silica. LPBF and LDED cross sections were prepared as single longitudinal
sections containing the build direction.





5Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy
(EDS) were performed on a Mira3 (Tescan, Brno, Czech Republic) with an Apollo X
detector (EDAX, Mahwah, NJ, USA)at 30 kV. Elemental maps were used to assess
compositional homogeneity in both powder and additively manufactured material.
Powder compositions are reported as atomic-number, absorption, and fluorescence
(ZAF)-corrected means of six-point analyses of particle cross-sections. The reported
uncertainty is the 1σ SmartQuant Error% returned by the software. LPBF and LDED
compositions are means over multiple areas or line scans per condition, with
uncertainties as standard deviations. Nb Lα and Zr Lα peak overlap was deconvolved
within the ZAF-corrected SmartQuant routine.

Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) was performed on a Tescan Mira SEM
equipped with an EDAX DigiView camera, acquired at 30 kV with a 1 µm step size,
and analyzed using EDAX OIM Analysis 7.3 software. Grain boundaries were defined
by a 15° misorientation threshold.

X-ray diffraction maps were collected on the cross sections of LPBF and LDED using
the custom-built Swissmapper instrument at Empa, on a regular grid with 500 µm
spacing. For each specimen an average diffraction pattern was calculated from all
measurement positions lying well inside the specimen boundary, comprising at least
28 positions. The diffractometer operates in fixed-angle reflection geometry with an
incidence angle of 17.5° and an exposure time of 20 s per position. The incident Cu
Kα beam (50 kV, 1 mA) was focused to a spot size of 150 µm using ASTIX optics
(AXO DRESDEN GmbH), giving a sample footprint of approximately 270 µm
equivalent circular diameter. Patterns were recorded on a stationary EIGER2 1M two-
dimensional detector (Dectris AG) covering a 2θ range of 30 to 120°. The         Pre-proof
experimental geometry was calibrated in pyFAI using LaB6 standard reference
material (NIST SRM 660c). Raw two-dimensional images were azimuthally integrated
into one-dimensional profiles using 1000 bins in 2θ and 1000 bins in the azimuthal
angle χ, giving a 2θ resolution of approximately 0.095°.

Grain size is reported as the area-weighted mean equivalent circle diameter (ECD)
from the OIM Analysis grain reconstruction, with edge grains excluded. Grain
elongation was quantified separately by a directional linear intercept method (Heyn,
ASTM E112 [25]) on the reconstructed boundary maps, using parallel and transverse   Journal
test lines at a nominal 10 µm spacing. The aspect ratio AR = L∥/L⊥ is the ratio of
mean intercept lengths parallel and transverse to the build direction, so AR > 1
indicates elongation along the build direction, edge grains were included in the
intercept count.

The PSD was measured by laser diffraction on a Mastersizer 3000+ Pro (Malvern
Panalytical, Malvern, UK; range 0.1 to 2500 µm) in dry dispersion with the Aero S
adapter. Particle size is the volume-equivalent spherical diameter, reported as the
D10, D50, and D90 percentiles of the cumulative volume distribution.

Nanoindentation was performed using a ZHN nanoindenter (ZwickRoell, Ulm,
Germany) equipped with a Berkovich diamond tip (Synton MDP, Switzerland) and
operated in load-controlled mode using a fast hardness protocol without continuous
stiffness measurement. Before testing, the tip area function was calibrated on a fused
silica reference. A maximum load of 5 mN was applied, with loading and unloading
rates of 10 mN s-1 and a dwell time of 1 s at maximum load. Indents were spaced
5 µm apart and arranged in line scans spanning the top to the bottom of each



6sample. Three line scans were acquired per sample, and sample preparation
followed the metallographic procedure described above for microstructural analysis.
1000 µm measured from the deposit surface was retained for bulk property
extraction. Hardness (H) and reduced elastic modulus (Er) were determined from the
load-displacement data using the Oliver–Pharr method [26]. Per-row outliers were
rejected by retaining values within the kernel-density-estimated peak ± 2σ at the half
maximum of each row, and H and Er were then averaged across the three line scans
at each indent position. Young's modulus E was computed from Er using a single
sample Poisson's ratio νs = 0.34, which lies within the ν = 0.30 to 0.38 range reported
for Nb, Ti, and Zr [27], together with the diamond indenter constants Ei = 1141 GPa
and νi = 0.07.

Novel titanium‑based sulfur‑containing BMG for PBF‑LB/M

Hanna Schönrath1     · Jan Wegner1,2 · Maximilian Frey3 · Martin A. Schroer2,4 · Xueze Jin5 ·
María Teresa Pérez‑Prado6 · Ralf Busch3 · Stefan Kleszczynski1,2


Received: 29 April 2024 / Accepted: 7 May 2024 / Published online: 25 May 2024
© The Author(s) 2024

Abstract
This paper investigates the additive manufacturing route for a novel glass-forming titanium-based sulfur-containing alloy of
the composition Ti60Zr15Cu17S8 . This system is a promising candidate for medical devices since the lack of toxic components
is combined with a high corrosion resistance and strength. Preliminary experiments and simulations show a general
processability of bulk material by powder bed fusion technologies. TEM and XRD reveal an amorphous microstructure of
laser-treated surfaces. Ultrasonic atomization is used to fabricate a flowable powder feed stock with spherical morphology and
crystalline microstructure, which is suitable for processing in powder bed fusion. Correlations between detected crystalline
phase formations and melt pool dynamics are revealed by SEM and EDX. It is shown that bulk samples with a high relative
density and partially crystalline microstructure can be manufactured.

 ORIGINAL ARTICLE


Recycling of Ti-15Mo and Ti-13Nb-13Zr alloys and their use in additive
manufacturing

Eliška Galčíková1     · Jan Krčil1 · Vladimír Mára1 · Lucie Pilsová1 · Jana Sobotová1 · Zdeněk Míchal2 · Dalibor Vojtěch3 ·
Jiří Režnar4


Received: 3 December 2025 / Accepted: 20 February 2026 / Published online: 14 March 2026
© The Author(s) 2026

Abstract
Recycling of titanium alloys represents a modern and economically attractive processing route, as it enables a significant
reduction in production costs associated with the high price of titanium. However, the properties of recycled β-titanium
alloys have not yet been sufficiently investigated in the scientific literature, and their potential for processing by additive
manufacturing technologies remains largely unexplored. This study focuses on evaluating the recycling of Ti-15Mo and
Ti-13Nb-13Zr alloys using the horizontal plasma arc melting (HPAM) method and further examines subsequent process­
ing steps, including hot working to the required shape for atomisation and subsequent powder processing via the LPBF
technique. In all technological stages, the microstructure was characterised, chemical analysis was performed, and, where
applicable, mechanical properties were evaluated. The results demonstrate that recycling of the investigated alloys is
feasible, as is their subsequent processing up to the production of additively manufactured specimens. Nevertheless, strict
control of the oxygen content is critical for both alloys, as the current levels exceed the limits specified by the relevant
standards. At such elevated oxygen concentrations, the alloys are unsuitable for biomedical applications; however, their
use in structural applications remains realistic, particularly considering the production cost reduction achieved through
the implementation of recycling.

Keywords  Ti-15Mo · Ti-13Nb-13Zr · Recycling process · Laser powder bed fusion

Abstract

   In this study, powder metallurgy methods were used to fabricate Mg-7.5Li-3Al-Zn alloys from repowdered extruded alloys. Extruded
alloys were powdered using ultrasonic atomization, and then laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) and pulse plasma sintering (PPS) were used
to consolidate the bulk materials. A comparison of the properties of the fabricated alloys with those of a conventionally extruded one was
carried out using methods that characterized the microstructure and corrosion resistance. When compared to their conventionally extruded
counterpart, LPBF and PPS materials exhibited reﬁned microstructures with low enrichment in AlLi and coarse Al, Zn, Mn precipitates. The
main drawback of the LPBF alloy, printed for the needs of this study, was its porosity, which had a negative effect on its corrosion. The
presence of unrecrystallized particle boundaries in the PPS alloy was also unbeneﬁcial with regard to corrosion. The advantage of the LPBF
and PPS processes was the ability to change the proportion of α(Mg) to β(Li), which when the complete consolidation of the material is
achievable, may increase the corrosion resistance of dual-structured Mg-Li alloys. The results show that powder metallurgy routes have a
wide potential to be used for the manufacture of Mg-Li based alloys.

Abstract:
Over recent years, ultrasonic atomization, especially with regard to liquid metals, has become an object of increased interest, mainly from industry, for additive manufacturing, but also from investigators, for research purposes. A strong correlation between the average particle size, distribution of particle sizes, and other process parameters like frequency and vibration amplitude was noted based on the analysis of available theoretical studies, simulations and experiments. The influence of parameters of the atomized fluid-like viscosity and surface tension on process parameters was also mentioned. The objective of this study is further research on the feasibility of using ultrasonic atomization to examine the properties of liquids, especially metals in liquid state. It attempts to close a gap in existing knowledge in searching for a new, possibly simple and cost-effective method to study the properties of liquid metals and further clarify the relationship between ultrasonic atomization parameters (amplitude, frequency, characteristics of metal being spilled on a vibrating surface) and obtained atomization results meant by average particle size and atomization time. Using numerical modeling (finite element method and computational fluid dynamics) as a methodology, combined with tests of using ultrasonic atomization as an instrument to determine properties of liquid metals, was considered as an introduction to a series of experiments. These tests were followed by real experiments that are also presented. At the first stage, numerical modeling was applied to a case of a specific liquid being spilled over a vibrating surface of different angles of inclination and specified, constant frequency and amplitude. The results of the simulation are in line with the current state of knowledge about ultrasonic atomization. Moreover, they can provide some more information on scalability, thus easing the comparison of the results of other experiments presented in the available literature. As a result, the relationship between fluid properties and the average size of atomized particles was demonstrated independently of the surface inclination angle. In the same way, the dependence of successful atomization on a sufficiently thin layer of a liquid was demonstrated. Thirdly, a correlation between the aforementioned layer thickness and the value of vibration amplitude has also been shown. Taking all the above into consideration, ultrasonic atomization can also be considered a research method and can be applied to study the properties of liquid metals. Further research, simulations and experimentation will be conducted to verify, develop and describe this method in full.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Additive manufacturing (AM) technologies have advanced from rapid prototyping to becoming viable manufacturing solutions, offering users both design flexibility and mechanical properties that meet ISO/ASTM standards. Powder bed fusion using a laser beam (PBF-LB), a popular additive manufacturing process (aka 3D printing), is used for the cost-effective production of high-quality products for the medical, aviation, and automotive industries. Despite the growing variety of metallic powder materials available for the PBF-LB process, there is still a need for new materials and procedures to optimize the processing parameters before implementing them into the production stage. In this study, we explored the use of a checkerboard scanning strategy to create samples of various sizes (ranging from 130 mm3 to 8000 mm3 using parameters developed for a small 125 mm3 piece). During the PBF-LB process, all samples were fabricated using Ti grade 2 and were in situ alloyed with a precisely controlled amount of oxygen (0.1–0.4% vol.) to enhance their mechanical properties using a solid solution strengthening mechanism. The samples were fabricated in three sets: I. Different sizes and orientations, II. Different scanning strategies, and III. Rods for high-cycle fatigue (HCF). For the tensile tests, micro samples were cut using WEDM, while for the HCF tests, samples were machined to eliminate the influence of surface roughness on their mechanical performance. The amount of oxygen in the fabricated samples was at least 50% higher than in raw Ti grade 2 powder. The O2-enriched Ti produced in the PBF-LB process exhibited a tensile strength ranging from 399 ± 25 MPa to 752 ± 14 MPa, with outcomes varying based on the size of the object and the laser scanning strategy employed. The fatigue strength of PBF-LB fabricated Ti was 386 MPa, whereas the reference Ti grade 2 rod samples exhibited a fatigue strength of 312 MPa. Our study revealed that PBF-LB parameters optimized for small samples could be adapted to fabricate larger samples using checkerboard (“island”) scanning strategies. However, some additional process parameter changes are needed to reduce porosity.</jats:p>

    methods on the Amazemet RePowder machine

        Kiyaasha Dyal Ukabhai1*, Donald Mkhonto1 and Maje Phasha1

        1Advanced Materials Division, Mintek, South Africa


                   Abstract. Additive manufacturing  is an important means of product
                      prototyping and main production process such as in jewelry where shaping
                may be difficult. With most powders being imported and expensive, there is
                    need to locally produce powder from extracted metal, scrap materials and
                     used powders for additive manufacturing. Al-10Cu (wt%) rod and powder
                   were prepared using the Amazemet rePowder system. A 90:10 by mass mix
                      of pure aluminium and pure copper was used as feedstock for both rod and
                    powder. The rod was melted using arc melting and the powder was produced
                   by ultrasonic induction atomisation. The rod and powder were analysed
                      using XRD and SEM. Results shows the same composition, phases and
                       microstructure were achieved in the rod and powder forms of the Al-10Cu

     1 Introduction

        Additive manufacturing (AM) is a rapidly growing industry around the world. One of the
        most used feedstocks for AM is spherical metal powder [1, 2, 3]. South Africa has an
        abundance of mineral resources [4], unfortunately, when metal powder feedstock is needed
         for AM, it has to be imported. Importing is not only costly in terms of price but also time
        wise as the lead times are long. Thus, to support the small scale development of the local
         additive manufacturing market, there is a need to create capability and capacity producing
         suitable powders locally. These powders need to be of high quality, with specific particle size
        and shape, depending on the type of AM technology. Often when a build is incomplete or
          results in an unsatisfactory product, the part is scrapped. In addition, especially with powder
        bed AM processes, there is scrap powder that cannot be reused. If these waste materials can
        be recycled into re-usable powder, it would lead to reduction of life cycle waste material for
     AM processing.
        Common types of atomiaation are gas, plasma and water atomisation. Gas atomisation is
         currently one of the leading methods for LPBF feedstock [5]. Gas atomisation is the process
         in which the liquid metal is dispersed by a high-velocity jet of air, nitrogen, argon, or helium
          [3]. The drawback of gas atomisation is that is requires high volumes of gas, at high pressure
        where, the particle size distribution (PSD) is controlled by the gas pressure. Current gas
         atomisation systems are limited by the melting temperature of the required powder alloy.
         Similarly, water atomisation depends on jets of water which hit a stream of liquid metal and

       form particles. The cons of the latter are that the particles can oxidize when they encounter
         the water, the particles are not all spherical and have porosity due to rapid cooling caused by
         the water jet [5, 6, 7].
          The Amazemet rePowder system allows one to make powder by ultrasonic atomisation
        using different feeds and has three different processing systems: induction module, arc
       module and wire feeding module [8]. From this PSD d50 = 15-75 µm can be produced which
           is suitable for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) printing [2, 9]. Rods or buttons can be made
        using arc melting module. Melting and powder production can be done using the arc module
         for high melting temperature alloys or induction module which uses bottom pouring
        technique for alloys with melting temperature up to 1300°C under inert environment. The
        machine uses ultrasonic energy to atomise the molten metal into powder. Ultrasonic
         atomisation is a process where a liquid is broken down into a fine mist of droplets by exposing
             it to a vibrating surface (sonotrode) emitting ultrasonic frequencies [10]. With the Amazemet
        rePowder system any form of material can be broken down into pieces and melted into rods
         or wire to be atomised. The powder formed is spherical and this is preferred for LPBF, as
         spherical particles have better flowability, reduced porosity and enhanced packing density
         [11]. A study done by Balasz et. al. [12] compared gas and ultrasonic atomisation for a
      common alloy Ti6Al4V, they found that the powder from ultrasonic atomisation gave a better
        production yield, good sphericity, good flowability and high density. Balasz et.al. also noted
          that the PSD for ultrasonic atomized powder is narrower than gas atomisation [12].
          The purpose of the study was to evaluate the Amazemet rePowder production processes
        while producing an aluminium- 10 (wt%) copper (Al-10Cu) alloy in rod and powder form.
       The composition was selected as it is known to be used in the automotive and aviation
         industry, however it must be noted that the alloy is not usually used in its cast form and
         usually has post processing steps [13]. Certain grain structures of materials like Al-Cu alloys
        can be useful in different applications, for example mechanical properties of intermetallic
         phases. Pure copper and aluminium pellets were used as the initial feedstock materials as
         these metals are affordable and readily available. The microstructures and phases that formed
          after casting the rod using the arc melting and using the induction furnace and ultrasonic
         atomisation to produce the powder were studied.

     2 Experimental procedure

        Experiments were carried out using the Amazemet rePowder system (Figure 1). The system
         uses a highly controlled inert environment within the chamber to melt alloys of any
        composition. Ultrasonic vibration atomisation technique is used to make powder from rods,
         buttons or wire that can be used for AM. This system has two options in which melting of
         material can be conducted: an induction furnace and an arc melting chamber. The induction
        furnace can currently melt materials under inert gas atmospheres with melting temperatures
       up to 1300°C whereas the arc melting chamber can handle up to 3500°C and both operate
        under vacuum. The composition of Al-10Cu (wt%) was chosen as it is a known alloy. It is
        expected that the alloy will have two phases: α-Al solid solution and θ-phase Al2Cu
         intermetallic compound [14-17].

Keywords:                                         Laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB) produced aluminium alloy components have attracted growing attention over
Laser powder bed fusion                            the past two decades due to their lightweight nature and excellent thermal and corrosion properties. However,
Synchrotron X-ray imaging                       few studies have examined the impact of substrate composition and microstructure. Using a high-performance
Microstructure                                               Al-Ni-Ce-Mn-Fe alloy (PA1) designed for additive manufacturing, we performed a series of single-track PBF-LBIntermetallics                                               experiments on as-cast PA1 and as-rolled Al6061 substrates to study their impact on track quality. Microstruc­Defects
                                                      tural analysis shows that, in optimal conditions, PBF-LB of PA1 produces very fine eutectic cells (~200 nm)
                                              without defects. Conversely, the as-cast PA1 substrate contains large columnar intermetallics, which have a
                                                  strong influence on defect formation during PBF-LB during initial layers. Such influence diminishes with
                                                   increasing build height due to microstructure homogenisation. However, the identified intermetallic-induced
                                               (IM) pore formation suggests a broader relevance beyond the present system, such as alloys form intermetallic
                                            under AM conditions or additive repair. We reveal and quantify the effects of print parameters and substrate
                                                 microstructure on defect formation during PBF-LB of PA1 using high-speed synchrotron X-ray imaging. Our
                                                        results show a new defect type, termed intermetallic-induced pores, arising from interactions between the
                                              keyhole and the pre-existing intermetallics. By quantifying different melting modes and defect types, we establish
                                             a process map and propose defect-lean printing strategies for PBF-LB of PA1.

## 1. ciftcli2025alloydevelopmentfrom pages 1-3 (Context ID: pqac-00000108)

J. Jpn. Soc. Powder Powder Metallurgy, 72 (2025) S729-S735
https://doi.org/10.2497/jjspm.15E-SIS13-03                                                                         S729
©2025 Japan Society of Powder and Powder Metallurgy


    Alloy Development From Sustainable Materials – Close-Loop Of Materials Using Ultrasonic
                                       Atomization

   Jakub CIFTCIi1,2 *, Tomasz CHOMA1,2, Bartosz MOROŃCZYK1,2, Bartosz KALICKI1,2, Filip PUCHALSKI1 and
                                       Łukasz ŻRODOWSKI1

             1AMAZEMET Sp. z o. o. [Ltd.], Al. Jana Pawła II 27, 00-867 Warsaw, Poland
 2Warsaw University of Technology, Faculty of Materials Science and Engineering, Wołoska 141, 02-507 Warsaw,
                                               Poland

    Abstract
    Current methods for the production of spherical powders restrict the development of new chemical compositions dedicated to the
    additive manufacturing industry. This novel ultrasonic atomization process enables in-house powder production from even one gram
   up to a few kilograms to verify new alloys. The technology use vibrations to break the surface tension of liquid metal to allow
    atomization. To melt the material plasma torch or induction heating can be used allowing to process wide range of metals.
    Plasma-based ultrasonic atomization was used to manufacture spherical powder of a high-temperature alloy, while induction-based
    ultrasonic atomization was used to develop a low-melting alloy. Additional case study of recycling titanium alloy maching chips into
    the powder by arc melting and ultrasonic atomization is presented.

   Keywords: Ultrasonic atomization, alloy development, additive manufacturing, custom powder production, recycling

    Introduction
    Metal powders are widely used in novel production methods, like laser powder bed fusion1), electron beam melting2), or direct energy
    deposition3). Additive manufacturing often requires materials with high flowability, and high packing density resulting in the need for
    spherical powders. The morphology limits the number of powder manufacturing methods that can be used for these processes. The
  AM industry mainly uses powders obtained by gas atomization4), water atomization5), and plasma/induction spheroidization6). These
    technologies allow for mass-production of powders. However, they are not conducive alloy development in AM due to costs
    associated with production changeover, requirements for specific feedstock types, and space requirements which do not allow the
     installation of such systems at research institutes or Universities. This results in the necessity to use powder blends7) or non-spherical
    powders8) influencing the homogeneity of chemical composition, and flowability.

    Ultrasonic atomization solves this issue thanks to the usage of vibration to break the surface tension of liquid metal to form droplets
     that solidify in a free-flow manner9). The absence of a high-velocity fluid stream such as in gas or water atomization allows for
    scaling down the atomization chamber. The ability for the melting mechanism to produce liquid metal in the moment of contact with
    the sonotrode allows it to work with any feedstock type without interfering with alloy development due to the complex process of
    feedstock preparation, like powder10) or wire11). Ultrasonic atomization was successfully used to obtain custom powders with tailored
    chemical composition: Zr-based alloy for bulk metallic glass formation during laser powder bed fusion12), platinum-based superalloy
    Pt84-Al11-Cr3-Ru2 for high-temperature applications13), AZ31B magnesium alloy modified with lithium to reduce its density14),
   aluminum 5754 alloy for automotive industry15), as well as functional material like Ni-Mn-Ga Heusler alloy with magnetocaloric
     properties16).

   C103 is a refractory-based niobium alloy for high-temperature applications like rocket propulsion systems and hypersonic missiles.
   The first use of this alloy was in Apollo Lunar Command Module rocket nozzles. Due to its main usage as thin-walled geometries
    and hard-to-machine nature, the examination of its usability in AM was launched. It was found that additively manufactured C103
    can achieve properties at ambient and 1093°C temperature required by ASTM B655 and can surpass the ultimate tensile strength of
     its wrought counterpart17).

   Magnesium alloys are extensively studied for orthopedic implants, which do not require removal thanks to their biodegradable
    properties without toxic ion release that can cause metallosis18). To adjust their corrosion rate to the bone tissue healing rate elements
     like silver can be used which additionally can result in an antibacterial effect of the lattice structures19).

    Titanium alloys are commonly used in aviation and aerospace application due to their high strength to weight ratio. Close loop of
    such materials is critical for sustainable research, especially concerning their strategic usage.

    In this article, ultrasonic atomization results of niobium C103 (Nb-10Hf-1Ti) alloy, magnesium alloy modified with silver and
    recycling of the titanium machining chips will be presented.
    *corresponding author, E-mail: jakub.ciftci@amazemet.com



This paper is licensed under Creative Commons (CC BY-NC-ND). If the further information is needed for this license, please visit the following website,
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/deed.en                                                                 March, 2025S730

    Experimental
    Ultrasonic atomization was carried out on rePOWDER (Amazemet, Poland). C103 niobium alloy was atomized from narrow sheet
     strips using a TZM rod sonotrode with a diameter of 30 mm which vibrated with a 40 kHz frequency. The ultrasonic vibrations,
    delivered through a sonotrode, create a standing wave on the surface of the sonotrode, which is transferred to the molten metal. By
    reaching the threshold amplitude, the internal forces of the liquid are broken, ejecting droplets of molten metal that solidify in an
    argon atmosphere. The chamber in which atomization was conducted is presented in Figure 1.





                                Figure 1 Chamber of rePOWDER in which C103 alloy was atomized

   The ultrasonic atomization of magnesium alloy was carried out using induction melting of the material in the crucible from which it
   was poured by the over-pressure control of argon after lifting the sealing rod, which was closing the nozzle opening. The stream of
    liquid metal contacts the 100 mm long vibrating blade operating at a frequency of 60 kHz. Due to the low density of magnesium
    alloy which caused mist formation in the chamber (Figure 2A) induction-based ultrasonic atomization of copper alloy is presented in
    Figure 2B to demonstrate the process. The phenomenon of ultrasonic atomization was described in detail in previous work9). Mg
    alloy contained Zn whose boiling point is 1180 K, which is too low temperature to melt Mg-1%Ag. To avoid significant Zn
    evaporation related to overheating the material to melt silver in the crucible master alloy was prepared using rePOWDER
    (Amazemet, Poland) arc melting module. Measured masses of  silver and Mg alloy rods were melted in the cold crucible
    (water-cooled copper plate) using plasma. The decrease in weight was noticeable due to the evaporation of volatile elements however
    for fast alloy screening own preparation of master alloy based on alloy with 25% Ag resulted in smaller deviations from theoretical
    composition than using commercial MgAg master alloy, especially as a small amount was needed to obtain 1% silver in the final
    powder. This had a beneficial effect on the sustainable consumption of available resources. The material after joining the matrix with
     silver pellets prior to homogenization is presented in Figure 3A and the homogenized custom master alloy in Figure 3B.





                   A                                      B
      Figure 2 Ultrasonic atomization of stream of alloy melted in the crucible using induction: (A) novel Mg alloy modified with silver
                             forms mist, and (B) copper alloy forms focused flow of atomized particles





                                                     “Journal of the Japan Society of Powder and Powder Metallurgy” Vol. 72 Supplement                                                                                                           S731





     Figure 3 Arc melting of Mg alloy with silver: (A) Mg alloy joined with visible silver pellets during processing with lowered current
                                       settings, and (B) homogenized master alloy (length is around 120 mm)

    Titanium maching chips were used to prepare ingots via arc melting and then atomized using

                             forms mist, and (B) copper alloy forms focused flow of atomized particles

     Figure 3 Arc melting of Mg alloy with silver: (A) Mg alloy joined with visible silver pellets during processing with lowered current
                                       settings, and (B) homogenized master alloy (length is around 120 mm)

    Titanium maching chips were used to prepare ingots via arc melting and then atomized using the same setup as for C103 alloy with
    reduced plasma torch parameters to avoid evaporation of Al from the alloy.

   SEM observations with EDS analysis were conducted using Hitachi SU8000 (Hitachi, Japan) and Axia ChemiSEM (Thermo Fischer,
    United States). Particle size distribution was measured using Litesizer DIA 500 (Anton Paar, Austria).

    Results and discussion
    Scanning electron microscopy revealed the spherical morphology of the C103 powder and its dendritic structure which was formed
    during the cooling stage of ultrasonic atomization. The powder was characterized by narrow particle size distribution and high
    sphericity factor (Figure  4). Such material will be characterized by advantageous bulk density and flowability beneficially
    influencing the powder bed fusion processes20).





                     Figure 4 SEM image of niobium C103 alloy powder: (A) macroscopic view, and (B) its structure

    During the inspection of the cross-section, HfO2 precipitates were not detected using EDS. Oxygen can highly impact the material
    performance which  is mainly used in critical applications21). EDS analysis of the cross-section of the powder confirmed no
    segregation of the elements in the observed scale.





March, 2025S732





                     C                                   D
      Figure 5 Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy: (A) combined elements, (B) Niobium detection, (C) Hafnium detection, and (D)
                                                      Titanium detection
    Induction-based ultrasonic atomization of the resultant magnesium alloy revealed the presence of submicron particles on the surface
    of particles with desired particle size distribution for laser powder bed fusion (Figure 6). The formation of submicron particles might
    be due to a melting temperature of 1223 K which causes evaporation of zinc and its deposition on the Mg alloy particles during
     solidification and cooling stages22). The high temperature was required to obtain a stable flow of the material. This also caused
     particle bonding. This phenomenon should be considered during the next trials. Using a nozzle with a larger diameter to maintain a
    stable dosage of material on the atomizing plate might allow reducing the pouring temperature of the modified alloy.





                                 Figure 6 Morphology of magnesium alloy powder modified with silver

    Ti-alloy chips from CNC machine were placed in the cold crucible made from copper. Using plasma torch, they were melted into the
    ingots (Figure 7A). Prepared feedstock was used for ultrasonic atomization using 40 kHz frequency. SEM observations revealed high
    sphericity of the material (Figure B). Dynamic Image Analysis revealed very narrow particle size distribution. D10, D50, and D90
    values are presented in table 1. Small amount of large particles are detected during volume – based analysis (Figure 8). Over 85 %
    atomized powder is below 100 microns which is suitable fraction for laser powder bed fusion, electron beam melting, hot isostatic
    pressing, and other powder-based manufacturing methods. The oxygen pickup during powder preparation was around 220 ppm
    comparing to the feedstock (overall oxygen was below 600 ppm which meets the ASTM F2924 standard).




                                                     “Journal of the Japan Society of Powder and Powder Metallurgy” Vol. 72 Supplement                                                                                                           S733

                     Figure 7 Ti-based powder atomized using ultrasonic atomization from recycled machining chips

                 Parameter                    Volume-based analysis (µm)            Number-based analysis (µm)
               D10                                36                                30
               D50                                49                                41
               D90                                118                                52

    Conclusions

     •   Ultrasonic atomization allows to obtain C103 niobium alloy with homogenous structure and morphology beneficial for additive
    manufacturing.
     •  When selecting the pouring temperature of Mg alloy during induction-based ultrasonic atomization possible evaporation of zinc
    and particle bonding must be considered.
     •  rePOWDER thanks to arc melting and ultrasonic atomization modules allow to recycling scraps
    of strategic materials like titanium alloy. As-atomized powder have narrow PSD which is suitable for additive manufacturing and
    other powder metallurgy methods.

                Abstract. The use of titanium alloys is growing fast as people have longer
                       life expectancies and small, customised, biomedical implants, especially in
                   dental applications, encourage the use of additive manufacturing (AM) to
                 shape them. The Ti-6Ta-1.5Zr-0.2Ru-5Cu (wt%) alloy has been identified
                   as a potential alloy for biomedical applications. Since laser powder bed
                  fusion (L-PBF) requires starting powders to be spherical and within a 10-
               100 µm  size  range, the Ti-6Ta-1.5Zr-0.2Ru-5Cu (wt%) powder was
                    ultrasonically atomised and then analysed by a Malvern Mastersizer, XRD
                and SEM-EDX to ascertain that it met the requirements of L-PBF.


   1 Introduction

     Titanium alloys are used in biomedical applications, including dental uses, due to their high
      strength, low Young’s modulus, excellent corrosion resistance and biocompatibility, and
      their  ability to bond with bone  (i.e. osseointegration)  [1]. The Ti-6Al-4V alloy and
     commercially pure titanium (CP-Ti) have been used in aerospace for engine components [2].
    Both these materials started to replace stainless steels and cobalt-based alloys in many
     biomedical applications since the 1970s [3] and are considered compatible due to their
     excellent combination of tensile and fatigue performance as well as biocompatibility [4].
    However, there are some concerns about Ti-6Al-4V since the alloying elements, aluminium
    and vanadium, are considered toxic [5], whereas CP-Ti does not have sufficient strength for
     load bearing implant applications [6].

       Using Ti-6Al-4V as the (α+β) reference, recent studies were done to replace Al and V
     with non-toxic elements for α+β stabilising, with zirconium and tantalum being proposed as
     the potential non-toxic alloying elements [7]. Copper was chosen because Cu additions to Ti
     alloys promote antibacterial properties [8, 9]. According to Liu et al. [9], the Cu content must

     The Ti-6Ta-1.5Zr-0.2Ru-5Cu (wt%) alloy was developed as a new potential (α+β) Ti alloy
      for dental applications [10]. Tantalum was chosen to replace V as a β stabiliser and Zr as a
      solution-hardening element, with Zr also contributing to the formation of a protective passive
      film to give good corrosion resistance [7]. Ruthenium was added to enhance corrosion
      resistance without changing the microstructure and is also non-toxic to living tissues [11].

         Additive manufacturing (AM) was developed four decades ago and more recently has
     become useful and cost effective for fabricating small, geometrically complex objects [12].
     The AM process involves fabrication of an object by depositing materials layer-by-layer
      following a three-dimensional model generated using computer-aided drawing. Hence, AM
      offers  the added advantage of  fabricating  fully compatible and accurate biomedical
     components [13]. Conventional methods (such as casting and powder metallurgy) require
      multiple steps which limit the time for modification of the final product, and it is difficult to
     produce complex shapes.

     AM includes different technologies; for this work, the laser powder-based fusion (L-PBF)
     method was selected because it can be used to manufacture almost all metal alloys and has a
     low direct cost [14]. L-PBF requires the starting powder to be spherical and within a typical
      size range of 15-45 µm for easy flowability and spreadability [15], although AMAZEMET
      stated that the powder could be in the size range of 10-100 µm [16]. The rePowder ultrasound
      atomisation system (AMAZEMET) was used to atomise the powder in small batches [16],
      using common laboratory conditions and can generate high purity spherical powders.

         Ultrasound atomisation is a liquid to solid process, where the material can either be melted
      in a crucible if the material is non-reactive and has a low melting point (e.g., Sn, Zn, Mg, Pb
     and Al alloys), and can be poured into the vibrating element or melted directly into the
     sonotrode if the material is highly reactive or has a high melting point (e.g., alloys based on
      Fe, Ti and Pt) [16]. The main principle of ultrasound atomisation depends on the amplitude
     and the surface wettability of the material [16]. Increasing the amplitude makes the liquid
      droplets smaller, and their size also depends on the frequency used and the properties of the
      liquid itself. These droplets are ejected from the melt within the thin film of liquid on the
     sonotrode surface [16]. The Particle Size Distribution (PSD) of ultrasound atomisation is
     narrow which means that up to 80% of the manufactured powder can be used [16]. The main
      factor that influences the PSD of the resulting powder is the frequency used. For L-PBF, a
     40 kHz frequency is suitable for powder with a D50 (average particle size) of 45-60 µm. The
      atomisation is carried under inert gas using an electric arc or focused plasma [17].


    2 Experimental procedure
     Pure elemental powders of:  Ti <45 µm, Ta < -60+100 mesh, Zr = APS 2-3 µm, Ru <45 µm
     and Cu <45 µm particle sizes were mixed in the ratio for Ti-6Ta-1.5Zr-0.2Ru-5Cu (wt%) for
     a total mass of 100 g. The powders were blended in a WAB T2C Turbula mixer to obtain a
     good mixture, followed by compaction with an Instron 1175 testing machine with the
    maximum load of 70 kN and cross-head speed of 20 mm/min. Ultrasonic atomisation was
     done using a rePower system [16], with a molybdenum alloy sonotrode at 40 kHz, with fixed
    155A current and 100-130% amplitude of the sonotrode at 180-280W, and 7 L/min argon gas
      flow, with the blower set at 13-17% maximum power. The whole process was carried out in
     an argon atmosphere. Powder produced was collected in an air lock container which was
      sealed in argon for safe handling. Fig 1. shows the rePower system used [16]. A Malvern

Abstract
Directed energy deposition (DED) additive manufacturing (AM) can fabricate, repair, and join
near-net-shaped components for high-performance engineering applications, including
biomedical, energy, and transport sectors. The broader adoption of DED remains constrained by
the limited number of alloys available that can be reliably manufactured without imperfections,
hence limiting mechanical properties. Here, we designed an Al–Ni–Ce–Mn–Fe AM alloy that
can achieve an ultra-fine microstructure (<5 µm), uniform distribution of intermetallics, low
residual stress (<32 MPa), and superior mechanical properties in as-built DED components.
Compared to DED AlSi10Mg in the as-built state using the same conditions, the yield increased
by 70%, and the ultimate tensile strength by 50%. DED-AM involves rapid cooling and
complex thermal conditions, which largely influence the property of the final components.
Post-characterization cannot capture the time resolved thermal behavior, hence offer limited
mechanism-based guide for alloy design. In this study, we develop a novel multimodal
characterization methodology for correlative in situ X-ray imaging, X-ray diffraction, and

## pqac-00000114

From text 'shu2024microstructureandmechanical pages 14-16'.

Zhiheng Shu and Yunzhong Liu. Microstructure and mechanical properties of a novel al-mg-sc-ti alloy fabricated by laser powder bed fusion. Materials, 17:686, Jan 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/ma17030686, doi:10.3390/ma17030686. This article has 6 citations.

The excerpt is a bibliography rather than a results section, so it does not provide mechanical-test values or a direct comparison between LPBF and directed energy deposition for PA1 Al-5.5Ni-4.6Ce-1.84Mn-0.3Fe-0.3Zr. It also contains no apparent reference to the PA1 composition. It does identify several potentially relevant aluminum LPBF mechanical-property papers and alloy systems. Monti et al. (Materials & Design, 2023, 229, 111907) is explicitly described as a new Al-Cu alloy for LPBF developed via ultrasonic atomization, making it the clearest additional qualifying powder-production paper in this excerpt. For Mg-containing systems, Cordova et al. study powder reuse in LPBF Al-Mg-Sc-Zr, while Spierings et al. report mechanical properties and heat-treatment effects in SLM Sc- and Zr-modified Al-Mg alloy. Other relevant alloy families include Al-Zn-Mg-Cu (Liu et al., 2022), AA7075 (Stopyra et al., 2020), Al-Mg-Zr (Croteau et al., 2018), and Al-Mg-Sc alloys, including TiB2-modified variants. These citations may support a review of Mg/Zn aluminum LPBF systems, but the excerpt alone cannot verify whether their powders were ultrasonically atomized, whether specimens were explicitly printed under the requested qualification, or how their strengths compare with DED.

Other cited studies concern Al-Cu-Mg-Ag-Ti-B, Al-Mg-Sc with calcium, Ti/Zr-modified Al-Mn, and Sc-modified aluminum alloys. These references may help expand the candidate literature set, but the excerpt alone supplies no evidence that their powders were produced by ultrasonic atomization, nor does it establish that each contains printed tensile/mechanical testing meeting the question’s criteria. ## pqac-00000116

From text 'ge2026laserscanningofinductionmelted pages 17-22'.

Zhaoxuan Ge, Sebastian Calderon, and S. Mohadeseh Taheri-Mousavi. Laser-scanning of induction-melted al-zr-er-ni alloys: are they representative of additively manufactured ones? Jun 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.matdes.2026.116142, doi:10.1016/j.matdes.2026.116142. This article has 2 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

Ge, Calderon, and Taheri-Mousavi provide a relevant comparative mechanical-testing study for an Al-Ni-Zr-Er alloy, although the excerpt does not establish ultrasonic atomization powder production and does not compare LPBF with directed energy deposition (DED). The work compares LPBF samples with induction-melted, laser-scanned bulk samples using Vickers hardness measured both parallel and perpendicular to the building direction. Both LPBF and laser-scanned specimens showed isotropic hardness, but the laser-scanned material was approximately 20% softer than the LPBF material; a benchmark alloy showed a similar 10% absolute decrease. The authors attribute the difference to phase-fraction variations and AM thermal histories that promote conversion of metastable phases into strengthening L12 precipitates. Microstructurally, laser-scanned samples closely reproduced LPBF grain-size distributions, precipitate populations, and nanoscale L12 core-shell precipitates, though melt-pool geometries differed and some inherited cast precipitates remained incompletely melted. This paper therefore supports the use of laser-scanned material for rapid alloy screening, while cautioning that hardness values are not directly interchangeable with LPBF values. It does not verify the requested PA1 Al-5.5Ni-4.6Ce-1.84Mn-0.3Fe-0.3Zr LPBF-versus-DED strength comparison, nor does it address Mg/Zn-Al systems.

The excerpt documents Ge, Calderon, and Taheri-Mousavi’s study comparing induction-melted, laser-scanned Al-Ni-Zr-Er material with an LPBF sample made using the same alloy system. It is relevant as a potential additional qualifying aluminum laser-powder-bed-fusion mechanical-testing paper, although the reported mechanical test is Vickers hardness rather than tensile strength, and the excerpt does not establish ultrasonic atomization of the powder. Hardness was measured both parallel and perpendicular to the building direction; both LPBF and laser-scanned specimens showed isotropic behavior. Laser-scanned samples were approximately 20% softer than the LPBF sample, with proposed explanations involving phase fractions and LPBF thermal history promoting metastable-to-L12 strengthening-phase transformation. A benchmark alloy comparison likewise showed a 10% absolute hardness difference. Despite substantially different melt-pool geometries, SEM/TEM observations showed similar cellular morphology, grain-size distributions, precipitates, phase distributions, and L12 nanoprecipitate core-shell structures. The article supports laser scanning as a rapid alloy-screening surrogate, but it does not verify the requested PA1 Al-5.5Ni-4.6Ce-1.84Mn-0.3Fe-0.3Zr LPBF-versus-directed-energy-deposition strength comparison, nor does it provide evidence about Mg/Zn-Al systems. Those claims require additional literature searches and full-text verification.

The excerpt provides background for identifying additional aluminum LPBF mechanical-testing papers, particularly studies involving compositionally modified or purpose-designed powders. It emphasizes that hot cracking remains a central limitation in LPBF aluminum and that alloy development or compositional modification is often required. Grain refiners and inoculants—including Ti, Zr, Sc, Er, TiB2, TiC, and related ceramic or carbon-based additions—are reported as strategies for producing fine equiaxed grains, improving liquid feeding, and reducing hot cracking. The passage specifically identifies Al-Mg-Sc Scalmalloy and Al-Cu-Ti A20X as alloys developed or optimized for PBF-LB/M, with reported combinations of strength, ductility, fatigue resistance, and corrosion or high-temperature performance. It also describes commercial RAM-modified alloys such as Al6061+RAM and Al7050+RAM, incorporating TiB2, Zr, and TiC nanoparticles, as well as Constellium’s Aheadd CP1 (Al-Fe-Zr) and HT1 (Al-Mn-Ni-Cu-Zr) powders. These systems may be useful comparison categories when reviewing ultrasonic-atomized powder LPBF studies and Mg/Zn-containing aluminum alloys. However, this excerpt does not mention PA1 (Al-5.5Ni-4.6Ce-1.84Mn-0.3Fe-0.3Zr), ultrasonic atomization, directed energy deposition, or comparative LPBF-versus-DED strength testing.

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)

Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.

before.description:

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):

        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1

        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment

forget to submit your answer.

Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.
