Printability

      The FR is the interval between the temperature at which the alloy is completely liquid and
the temperature at which it is 99 % solidified (𝐹𝑅= 𝑇3L −𝑇3.MML   ). As this temperature interval get
larger, the solidification dendrites are not fed with liquid and leads to shrinkage and thermal

contractions and finally cavities and hot cracking. Therefore, minimizing FR is essential to



                                                                                   15evaluate the HCS. Here, we also analyze HCS of the developed Al alloy by the model developed

by Clyne and Davis to evaluate the CSC51. According to this model, mass and liquid feeding start
from a normalized time 𝑡$ (0.6 to 0.1 volume fraction of liquid), in which stresses at the mushy
zone can be relaxed. However, the cracking-vulnerable time 𝑡N is defined from 0.1 to 0.01.
Consequently, the ratio 𝑡N/𝑡$ results in the CSC parameter. We obtained data for the FR and CSC
parameters by conducting nonequilibrium Scheil solidification simulations. To measure the CSC

parameter, we assumed that heat flow is proportional to the square root of time. Note that the high-

melting precipitation of rare earth elements significantly increases the FR. However, based on

experiments, these initial precipitations do not increase HCS. Thus, these precipitates are ignored

during the FR and CSC calculations. Therefore, to ensure printability of our Al alloy, we must

minimize the HCS, which is the product of FR and CSC1.

ML analysis

      Using the LHS random sampling technique, we generated 250,000 and 500,000 data. We
then used Thermo-Calc to perform single equilibrium calculations at 250°C61. The at. % of the

elements in L12 phases and Al matrix were extracted using the TC-python interface and fed into

Eq. 2. The at. % of the five elements in the composition constitutes our feature/input vector. We

normalized the input values by deducing the mean and scaling to the variance. We used the Cuml

library from RAPIDS62 developed by NVIDIA for the KNN, RF, SVR, GB, and LR techniques,

and TensorFlow for the NN regression technique. We divided the data into training (varying %)

and test datasets 20%. The hyperparameters associated with the ML techniques are presented in

Supplementary Table S1. They were optimized using grid search and 5-fold cross validation (80%

for training and 20% for validation) of the RMSE using gradient descent and Adam optimizers63.

The target predicted value was the coarsening metric of L12 phases. After defining the optimum

set of hyperparameters for each technique, we measured the prediction error on the test data set

for different percentages of the training data. NN regression showed the minimum RMSE

compared to other techniques at different percentages. We repeated the measurement 5 times for

various  initial seeds for NN and the minimum and maximum of the RMSE  is shown in

Supplementary Fig. S2 with error bars. The lower RMSE of NN is partially due to the fact that

the available hyperparameters in Cuml 3.2 are currently limited and the whole spectrum of

hyperparameters is not fully implemented. The NN regressor was thus used to forward predict

coarsening metrics used in inverse design techniques. We applied two inverse design approaches.



                                                                                   16First, we used BO with GP as a surrogate model and generated data using the NN regressor. As a

second method in this approach, we also calculated the labels of the data directly using the TC-

python interface of Thermo-Calc. In the second approach, we used PSO for the inverse design

technique and generated the labels of data from the NN regressor. GP was chosen as the surrogate

model for the BO as it has relatively low number of hyperparameters, our objective function is

continuous, and the uncertainty of the fitted model is known. The uncertainty defines the tradeoff

between exploration and exploitation in acquisition function of BO.

     SEM-BSE and SEM-EDS data were collected on a JEOL JSM7900F FE-SEM equipped

with an Oxford Ultim Max 100 mm2 detector. BSE images were collected at 5 kV and 20 kV to

optimize surface sensitivity and contrast, respectively. SEM-EDS data were also collected at 5 kV

and 15-20 kV, in order to prioritize spatial resolution of surface features at the lower voltage, and

to permit detection of the full suite of elements including Er at the higher voltage. EDS spectra

and maps were collected and processed using Aztec 5.1 software.

     SEM-BSE and SEM-EDS data of zero-nickel and induction-melted alloys were collected

on a ThermoFisher Apreo HiVac SEM equipped with an EDAX Elite 150 SDD EDS detector. The

BSE-EDS data were obtained at 15 kV in order to measure the presence of all elements and to

give the optimal spatial resolution on EDS maps. The EDS spectra and maps were processed by

EDAX APEX software.

     SEM-EBSD data of the top and side surface of our designed alloy were collected on a

ThermoFisher Apreo HiVac SEM equipped with an EDAX Hikari EBSD  detector. The

EBSD data were collected at 15 kV, and the step size was set to 0.045 μm to secure the spatial

resolution. The raw Kikuchi diffractograms were post-analyzed in OIM and home-developed

SphInx softwares64.

beam microscope (Thermo Fisher Scientific). After selecting a sample region containing a

representative collection of features of interest via backscatter electron imaging, we extracted a

micromanipulator (Oxford Instruments). Due to the large ion range of Ga ions in aluminum, which

APT of 3D-printed samples

    We prepared specimens for APT following standard lift-out methods, using a FEI Helios

660 dual-beam FIB/SEM. APT was performed with a Cameca LEAP 4000 HR, operated in

voltage-pulsing mode with the following experimental conditions: base temperature 40 K, pulse

rate 100 kHz, pulse fraction 15%, and detection rate 0.5%.

      Each LEAP dataset was reconstructed and analyzed using Cameca IVAS software version

3.6.14. We used SEM images of each LEAP tip to measure the shank half angle and tip radius;

these images were incorporated into the shape of the reconstruction. Two of the LEAP tips showed

a fine dispersion of Zr-rich precipitates, and one LEAP tip showed a large phase rich in Er and Ni.

The Zr-rich precipitates were segmented using isosurfaces set to 3.0% Zr (Fig. 6k). The Er- and

Ni-rich phase was segmented using an isosurface set to 2.5% Ni, as shown in Fig. 6l. The

reconstructions shown here illustrate the Zr = 3.0% isosurfaces and collection of Er and Ni in



                                                                                   18second phases, respectively. A proximity histogram concentration profile was applied to both

second phases and for all interfaces set by the isosurfaces (Figs. 6m & n). A bin size of 0.1nm

was used for both histograms.

      The composition of the matrix and fine precipitates were measured using two LEAP tips

segmented with Zr = 0.3 at. % isosurfaces, and the composition of the large second phase was

measured from the third LEAP tip (Supplementary Table S2). These measurements indicate that

the fine precipitates are the L12 phase, and the large second phase is the ternary Al-Ni-Er/Zr phase.

      Supplementary Fig. S5 shows the distribution of diffusion resistivity with respect to the

studied parameters: Ni, Er, Zr, Y, and Yb at. percentages; diffusion resistivity; misfit strain; and

the coarsening metric. Supplementary Fig. S5a shows that lowering the amount of Ni suppresses

normalized diffusion resistivity above 1.6 and below 0.1. Moreover, Er decreases the diffusion

resistivity when increased to 0.35 at. %. Further, high diffusion resistivities are for Er in 1.2-1.6

at. %. Moreover,  it is evident that Zr has a notable contribution to the increase in diffusion

resistivity. Analysis of the diffusion resistivity with respect to Y at. % shows that the highest values

are achieved when Y at. % ranges between 0.2 and 0.3. When Yb is increased, the diffusion

resistivity decreases initially from the maximum values throughout the range and appears to

distribute uniformly in the 0-1.65 range. Supplementary Fig. S6 shows the distribution of misfit

strain with respect to the studied parameters. The distributions do not indicate a specific correlation

between the at. % of alloying elements and the misfit strain. The distribution of misfit strain with

respect to coarsening metric shows that at lower coarsening metrics, the misfit strain also achieves

low values, as expected.

      Supplementary Fig. S7 shows the coarsening metrics with respect to the studied

parameters: Ni, Er, Zr, Y, and Yb at. %; diffusion resistivity; and misfit strain. These subplots

reveal that among alloying elements, Zr plays the most significant role in decreasing the coarsening

metric. Moreover, the initial increase of Er concentration from 0 to 0.4 at. % seems to increase the

range in the variation of coarsening metrics remarkably. Supplementary Figs. S7g and S7h show

that the coarsening metric is highly influenced by diffusion resistivity and is less influenced by

misfit strain.



                                                                                   20    We  also  analyzed L12  at. %  with  respect  to  studied  parameters. As shown  in

Supplementary Fig. S8, Er has the maximum contribution for the increase of this phase. In

contrast, an increase in Ni and Y decreases this phase.

Supplementary Discussion 2: Spearman coefficients

      The correlations between the studied parameters are shown in the heat map in Fig. 4. The

heat map represents the Spearman coefficient and indicates a linear correlation for each ranked

pair of parameters. The Spearman coefficient values are also presented in this figure. The

parameters show that, as expected, Zr has the greatest influence on the diffusion resistivity,

increasing it by 0.78; Yb has the inverse effect, decreasing it by 0.35. Er and Y rank second and

third, respectively, in terms of their influence on decreasing the bulk diffusion resistivity. Ni seems

to have no influence on this parameter. The fluence of these elements on coarsening metric is the

same but in reverse trend of their diffusion resistivity index. Finally, as can be seen from the

distributions in Supplementary Figs. S7g and S7h, the diffusion resistivity is more influential,

decreasing the coarsening metric (by 0.96) than the misfit strain (by 0.22).

     FR is mainly controlled by Yb, Er, and Ni. Yb negatively influences formation of eutectic

ternary phases and Ni influences on both eutectic ternary and Al3Ni phases. Er and Y have the

highest effects on CSC, while none of them can strongly change this parameter. To reduce the

HCS, additions of Er and Yb has the highest advantageous (by 0.51) and disadvantageous (by

0.50) based on the Spearman coefficients.

Supplementary Discussion 3: Uncertainty quantification for performance descriptors

       Uncertainty quantification was performed using the t-statistics test, a statistical measure

for hypothesis testing to determine whether a process to change has some impact on a feature of

interest. A method for this is the “one-tailed test” which determines if, for a distribution, the mean

value of a target value is greater than or less than an expected mean. This test is conducted by

                                                       QR*STQRU
calculating the critical “t” statistic as t = LVW(Q), where STD(θ) is the standard deviation of the
distribution, θG is the calculated mean of the sample set, and E(θG) is the expected mean value. The

tailed test relies on a null (Ho) and alternative (HA) hypothesis and compares the calculated statistic

against a known value (z), given the confidence interval and dataset size. The relation of the

calculated and known value determines if the null hypothesis can be rejected or accepted.



                                                                                   21      For this work, the test was applied to predict if variations in composition off the ML-

optimized design would have significant impacts on performance (as coarsening metric and

fraction of L12). The dataset was constructed by forming three normal distributions for Ni, Er, and

Zr, treating the composition of the design as the mean, and a 50% change as the standard deviation.

1250 values were sampled from each distribution to form the dataset, which were then modeled

our high throughput framework.

      The t-test was performed in two manners: by treating Ho as the mean L12 fraction being

greater than or equal to 95% that of the optimized design, μL12 > 0.95 L12,ML, (and HA as being less

than this value), and with Ho as the mean coarsening metric being less than or equal to 105% the

optimized design, μCmetric < 1.05 CmetricML. This structure was chosen to predict if a 5% loss in

performance is expected to occur on average.

for each distribution was calculated using the above equation and compared to the confidence

L12 values was found to be greater than this, indicating that with 99% confidence the null

the mean fraction of L12 is greater than or equal to 95% of the optimized design). Similarly, the

coarsening metric was significantly below the critical value, as such the null hypothesis could not

be rejected. The distributions of the simulated L12 fraction and coarsening metric are presented in

Supplementary Fig. S10.

Supplementary Discussion 4: Experiments on laser-scanned induction-melted samples to

validate printability and precipitation hardening

      For the experimental investigation of printability, we demonstrated an approach to

assessing the development of hot cracks as a function of chemical composition. First, we scaled

the 9 batches determined via ML using an XPR Analytical Balance (Mettler Toledo) with an

accuracy of 0.005 mg. The purity of the raw elements utilized in this study exhibited was as

follows: Al (99.99%), Ni (99.99%), Er (99.9%), and Zr (99.95%). The elements were employed

in granulate shape (<5 mm). For each batch, a total of 30 g was cast using the induction heating

system MC20V (Indutherm) to ensure a homogeneous elemental distribution in the Al2O3-

crucible.



                                                                                   22       Before heating, a vacuum was pumped to 0.1 mbar, reducing residual O2, then afterward

flooded with Ar to normal pressure. The melting chamber was subsequently flooded with Ar

sequentially to avoid oxidation during melting. The overheating temperature of the melts was

adjusted to 1000°C, at which full melting of raw elements was achieved. The holding time at this

melting temperature was  set to 5 min. The castings  solidified as rods with a length of

approximately 60 mm and a diameter of 15 mm. These rods were rolled to obtain sheets. The roll

gap was iteratively reduced over 10 steps to the desired thickness of 2 mm. During the rolling

procedure, the specimens were heated to 100°C to avoid edge cracking. Using this procedure, we

obtained sheets with a dimension of 280 × 35 × 2 mm3. Because rolling caused the sheets to bend

marginally, we performed a pressing step to produce flat sheets. The sheets were then laser

scanned using an LT30 LPBF machine (DMG MORI) on multiple paths mimicking one layer

printing of the powder. To ensure its performance and reliability, we generally calibrated the

LPBF machine according to ISO/ASTM DIS 52941:2019. This system is equipped with a solid-

state Nd: YAG laser source with a wavelength of 1064 nm and a maximum laser power of

1000 W. Additionally, the laser beam had a Gaussian distribution with an adjusted laser focus of

70 µm. Regarding the atmosphere in the build chamber, Ar -4.6 was used to reduce a residual O2

content to <1000 ppm.

      The baseplate temperature was set to room temperature and the baseplate was sprayed

with BN to avoid a potential joining of the sheets to the baseplate. The LPBF processing

parameters were used to ensure a deep penetration (~1.2 mm) by the laser. The following

combination of process parameters was determined based on preliminary studies: scan speed

300 mm/s, hatch distance 170 µm, and laser power 400 W. A region of 200 × 25 mm2 was laser-

scanned employing a stripe-scanning strategy with a vector length of 8 mm to minimize warpage

and residual stress in the Al-sheets. Both sides of the sheets were laser scanned to ensure the rapid

solidification  of  the  microstructure  throughout  the  processed  volume. To  validate  the

development of hot cracks during laser scanning, the specimens were extracted from the laser-

exposed region. The cut specimens were conductively embedded, ground, and polished using a

Hexamatic (Struers). Next, they were vibro-polished using a Vibromet (Bruker) via colloidal

suspension. Light micrographic images were then generated using a VHX 5000 (Keyence) to

detect undesired process-induced defects.





                                                                                   23      The mechanical properties of the laser-scanned sheets in as-built and aged for 8 hrs at

400°C were analyzed. As part of this process, micro-hardness of the sheets was measured using an

automatic Vickers hardness tester FA 30 (KB) applying 100 gram force loading. At least five

measurements on  the same sample were performed and  the  average  value  is  reported

(Supplementary Fig. S12). We further performed Vickers hardness tests on induction melted

sample of our final design: Ni = 1.33 at. % and Zr = 1 at. %. Ten measurements on the same

sample were performed and the average value and the standard deviation are shown  in

Supplementary Fig. S17.

Supplementary Discussion 5: 3D-printing of custom alloys

      The powder materials were ultrasonically atomized using an AUS500 system (Indutherm

Bluepower). For the induction melting, an Al2O3 crucible was coated with hexagonal boron nitride

paste to prevent the melt from reacting with the crucible material. The obtained particle size

distribution was measured by laser diffraction method. The particle size distribution for the ML-

optimized powder material was as follows: d10 = 44.5 %, d50 = 63.8 %, and d90 = 91.5 %. The

chemical composition of the powder material was measured for the ML-optimized Al-2.47Ni-

3.25Zr-2.38Er, which was detected via X-ray fluorescence measurement.

       Subsequently, specimens were additively manufactured via LPBF using an SLM Solutions

250 HL machine. This machine has an Nd:YAG laser with a maximum laser power of 400 W

operating at a wavelength of 1064 nm. We applied a Gaussian beam distribution with a laser beam

diameter of 70 µm. The following processing parameters were employed: laser power 350 W,

hatch distance 120 µm, scan speed 1100 mm/s, layer thickness 50 µm, scan strategy 8 mm stripes,

and rotation of 67°. Regarding the build chamber conditions, a preheating temperature of 200 °C

was selected, and during 3D-printing, Ar-4.6 was employed as an inert gas atmosphere with a

residual O2-level of < 1000 ppm. Additionally, before SLM processing, the powder materials were

vacuum dried to reduce their relative humidity by < 5 % using a system developed in-house. The

specimen geometry printed were with the dimensions of 6 mm3 and 2 cm × 6 mm × 6 mm. The

chemical composition of the printed ML-optimized specimens was Al-2.55Ni-2.9Zr-2.37Er

detected via X-ray fluorescence measurement.

samples

Atomic resolution imaging of these precipitates reveals a non-uniform composition and structure

suggest that these structures correspond with the predicted Al-Ni-Er ternary and the Al-(Zr/Er) L12

phases, respectively, as shown by EDS maps in Figs. 6d & e. In addition, similar L12-type

structures are found attached to

## 1. ekaputra2026coarseningandcreepbehavior pages 21-25 (Context ID: pqac-00000044)

s in the Al-Zr-Mo and -W alloys are 1-2 orders of magnitude lower
than that of the Al-Zr-Mn, -Cr, and -V alloys, and their threshold stresses for dislocation creep
are also higher by ~10 MPa. The hardness of the peak-aged alloys after creep testing (Fig. S5,
Supplementary Information) has slightly decreased, likely due to the long duration of the creep
tests (~100h) compared to the peak-aging treatment (4 h). However, the over-aged (400°C/504h)
alloys (Fig. 10(b)), where the over-aging treatment prior to creep is over 3x longer than the creep
test duration, exhibit no significant decrease in creep resistance compared to the peak-aged
alloys. The creep properties of the binary Al-Zr alloy do not significantly change after over-
aging. The Al-Zr-Mn and Al-Zr-Cr alloys are somewhat more creep resistant after over-aging,
with creep strain rates decreasing by <1 order of magnitude, and a mild increase in dislocation
creep threshold stress. The creep properties of the Al-Zr-V, -Mo, and -W alloys are not
significantly changed after over-aging.

The creep properties of the peak-aged binary Al-Zr and ternary Al-Zr-X alloys are also compared
to various cast and additively-manufactured alloys in the literature in Fig. 10(d), also tested at
400°C. The binary L-PBF Al-0.4Zr (at.%) alloy studied here is significantly more creep-resistant
than a cast Al-0.11Zr-0.005Er (at.%) alloy fabricated by gravity casting [18], likely due to the
higher Zr content in our alloy, likely due to the higher supersaturation of Zr in the matrix of our
alloy, which is enabled by the rapid solidification rates of L-PBF. We note that the Mo impurities
introduced by the atomization process likely also contribute to the creep resistance of ournominally binary Al-Zr alloy. Additions of slow-diffusing Mn solute were found to significantly
improve creep resistance in a cast Al-Mn-Zr-Er-Si alloy [18]; a similar effect is found by
additions of slow-diffusing Mn, Cr, V, Mo, or W solute in the present L-PBF Al-Zr-X alloys.
Several other creep-resistant Al-based alloys are plotted for comparison, including a cast Al-Cu-
Mg-Ag-Sc alloy strengthened by Sc-stabilized Cu-rich precipitates [41], as well as eutectic Al-
Ce-Ni-Fe [42], Al-Ce-Ni-Mn [43], and Al-Ce-Ni-Mn-Zr [44] alloys strengthened by >20 vol.%
of submicron eutectic phases formed during solidification. The Al-Zr-X alloys studied here,
containing just L12-Al3Zr precipitates and solid solutions of either Mn, Cr, V, Mo, or W, are
comparable in their creep properties at 400°C to these other alloys in the literature with much
higher volume fractions of strengthening particles and much higher alloying content. Figure 10. Double-logarithmic plot of minimum creep strain rates vs. applied stress during compressive creep at
400°C for binary Al-Zr and ternary Al-Zr-X alloys (a) in the peak-aged (400°C/4h) (b) and over-aged (400°C/504h)
conditions. Error bars estimated as ±50% for strain rates below 10-8 s-1, ±30% below 10-7 s-1, and ±20% above 10-7 s-
1, as in Ref. [45]. (c) Dislocation creep threshold stresses of peak-aged and over-aged Al-Zr and Al-Zr-X alloys.
Error bars are estimated as ±1 MPa. (d) Peak-aged alloys, with comparison to various creep-resistant aluminum
alloys in literature [18, 41-44].4. Discussion

4.1. Solute supersaturation in L-PBF Al-Zr-X alloys

Supersaturated solid solutions of Zr and the ternary alloying element X (Cr, V, Mo, and W) were
observed in both the binary Al-Zr and ternary Al-Zr-X alloys. These solid solutions were
observed directly via APT analyses (Fig. 5), and indirectly via SEM (Fig. 4) and electrical
conductivity analyses (Fig. 8). These supersaturated solid solutions are achieved in the L-PBF
Al-Zr-Cr, -V, -Mo, and -W alloys in concentrations beyond what was attainable in the arc-melted
alloys, due to the faster solidification rates in L-PBF..

The Al-Zr-Mn and -Cr alloys did not show obvious primary precipitates, unlike the Al-Zr-V, -
Mo, and -W alloys, which is attributed to the varying solidification intervals of these alloys. In
the Al-Zr-Mn alloy, a supersaturated solid solution was achieved in both the arc-melted and L-
PBF processed alloys. In the binary Al-Mn system, the solidification interval is quite small (1°C
for 1 at.% Mn, calculated via Thermo-Calc, TCAL8 database), and as a result little undercooling
is required to trap Mn in solution. This is consistent with the high amounts of Mn in solid
solution observed in the arc-melted Al-Zr-Mn alloy, as well as in other studies where as much as
~2 at.% Mn was retained in solution. For Al-Cr, the solidification interval is much larger (101°C
for 1 at.% Cr), which is qualitatively consistent with little solute supersaturation in the arc-
melted alloy, but much greater amounts in the L-PBF processed alloy. For Al-V, Al-Mo, and Al-
W, the solidification intervals are even larger (315, 205, and 375°C for 1 at.% V, Mo, W
respectively). In the L-PBF process, it is well-established that the solidification velocity and
cooling rates are lowest at the meltpool boundary, and fastest at the center of the meltpool [6].
As a result, the slower cooling rates at the meltpool boundaries are insufficient to fully suppress
primary Al-X precipitation in the V-, Mo-, and W-containing alloys, but the faster cooling rates
near the center of the meltpool are sufficient, as observed for primary Al3Zr precipitates in many
other Al-Zr based alloys [6, 7, 46].

These observations are consistent with previous results in the rapid solidification and L-PBF
literature. Fedorov and Elagin [14] studied supersaturation in binary Al-X alloys (the same
elements as studied here), where mm-size granules were cooled from the melt at a rate of 103-104
K/s. In their study, the maximum achievable solute supersaturation in various binary Al-X alloys
was 2.2% Mn, 0.94% Cr, 0.53% V, 0.18% Mo, and 0.18% W (at.%). For our Al-Zr-Mn and Al-
Zr-Cr alloys, the high supersaturation of Mn and Cr is consistent with the extended solubility for
these elements observed by the above authors [14] at 103-104 K/s. Other researchers have
studied rapid solidification of these binary Al-Mn [47] and Al-Cr [48-50] systems, and observed
even greater extended solutions (up to 5 wt.%) for both Mn and Cr. Mn and Cr have also been
studied in L-PBF processed alloys [8, 13, 51] and extended solid solutions of up to 4.5 wt.% Mn
and 3 wt.% Cr have been observed in L-PBF. In rapidly solidified Al-V, Al-Mo, and Al-W alloys
cooled at a rate of 105-106 K/s (similar to L-PBF), as much as 2 at.% V [15], 1.3 at.% Mo [16],
and 1.0 at.% W [17], which is consistent with the microstructures of the Al-Zr-V, -Mo, and -W
alloys at the center of the meltpool. However, the cooling rates at the meltpool boundary may be
insufficient to trap the amounts of V, Mo, and W added to these Al-Zr-X alloys. In Al-Mn-Sc
alloys with similar microstructure, the presence of primary Mn-rich intermetallic precipitatesnear the meltpool boundary can initiate failure there [52]. In these Al-Zr-X based alloys, it may
therefore be desirable to lower the ternary solute content for similar reasons, but more studies are
required to quantify the effect of solute content on mechanical properties.


4.2. Stability of supersaturated solid solutions with ternary solute

The supersaturated solid solutions of the Al-Zr-X alloys decompose during aging to form binary
Al-X precipitates, but at varying rates as evidenced by microstructural and electrical conductivity
investigations. From electrical conductivity studies (Fig. 8), sharp increases in conductivity
during aging at 400°C occurred after ~1 day in the Al-Zr-Mn alloy, after ~1 month in the Al-Zr-
Cr alloy, but were not observed in the Al-Zr-V, -Mo, or -W alloys after the longest time studied
here (2016 h or ~3 months). In the latter three alloys, the conductivity increases during aging at
a higher temperature (590°C) for 24h. These conductivity results are consistent with
microstructural studies (via SEM in Fig. 9, XRD in Fig. S4), which clearly show intragranular
precipitates in the Al-Zr-Mn alloy after 400°C/8h aging, in the Al-Zr-Cr alloy after 400°C/1008h
aging, and in the Al-Zr-V, -Mo, and -W alloys only after 590°C/24h aging.

The relative rates of precipitation align with the diffusivities of the ternary solute elements at
400°C (9 x 10-19 for Mn, 1.3 x 10-21 for Cr, and 5 x 10-24, 5 x 10-23, and 5 x 10-23 for V, Mo, and
W, in units m2/s [23]). We also compare here to existing experimental literature on rapidly-
solidified alloys containing these elements. During aging of rapidly solidified Al-1Mn (at.%)
alloys, weak Al6Mn peaks were detected after annealing at 450°C for 1h [47]. During isochronal
annealing (from 250-550°C, in 6h steps) of Al-1Cr (at.%) alloy fabricated by melt-spinning,
precipitation was observed to initiate after 6h at 500°C. While the aging procedures used in these
two studies [47, 49] are somewhat different, the higher initiation temperature for precipitation in
the Al-

tation align with the diffusivities of the ternary solute elements at
400°C (9 x 10-19 for Mn, 1.3 x 10-21 for Cr, and 5 x 10-24, 5 x 10-23, and 5 x 10-23 for V, Mo, and
W, in units m2/s [23]). We also compare here to existing experimental literature on rapidly-
solidified alloys containing these elements. During aging of rapidly solidified Al-1Mn (at.%)
alloys, weak Al6Mn peaks were detected after annealing at 450°C for 1h [47]. During isochronal
annealing (from 250-550°C, in 6h steps) of Al-1Cr (at.%) alloy fabricated by melt-spinning,
precipitation was observed to initiate after 6h at 500°C. While the aging procedures used in these
two studies [47, 49] are somewhat different, the higher initiation temperature for precipitation in
the Al-Cr alloy is consistent with the longer time required for precipitation at 400°C in our Al-
Zr-Cr alloy. During isochronal aging (1 h duration) of an Al-1.0 at.% Mo alloy, nanometric
precipitates were visible at 400°C, and more pronounced at 500°C [16]. In contrast, we did not
observe a significant change in resistivity due to Mo precipitation, nor did we observe any
nanometric Mo-rich precipitates via APT after 4h aging at 400°C. It is likely that the lower
content of Mo in solution measured in our alloy (~0.4 at.%, from APT analyses) reduces the
driving force for precipitation. Indeed, the kinetics of decomposition of the solid solution in all
these alloys will depend strongly on the amount of solute in solution, as observed in several other
studies [16, 17, 47-50]. Furthermore, although solute may not precipitate in grain interiors,
precipitation will occur more quickly at grain boundaries, even for the more slow-diffusing V,
Mo, and W solutes (as observed in previous studies in rapidly-solidified alloys [16, 48, 49]).

Although the rates of precipitation are different in the varying ternary alloys, this does not appear
to have a significant effect on the mechanical properties of these ternary Al-Zr-X alloys, as
discussed in the following sections.4.3. Room-temperature strengthening mechanisms

The room-temperature strength of the binary Al-Zr and ternary Al-Zr-X alloys reflect
contributions from both Zr and the ternary solute element, each of which provides strengthening
by a combination of solid-solution and precipitation hardening.

We first estimate the strengthening contributions from Zr to the hardness of the alloys (all
calculations are provided in Supplementary Information). The maximum solid-solution
strengthening contribution from Zr, assuming it is fully in solution (using SEM-EDS
measurements in the as-fabricated binary Al-Zr alloy as the maximum possible Zr solute
concentration, Table 1), is ΔHVZr,SS = 44 MPa. To estimate the precipitation strengthening
contribution, we take APT data for the peak-aged alloys, and assume an average precipitate
radius of ~1.3 nm and volume fraction of 0.33% (Table 2). Then, the L12-Al3Zr is predicted to be
bypassed by shearing, and controlled by coherency and modulus strengthening (based on
equations previously applied to L12-strengthened Al alloys in Ref. [53], with detailed
calculations given in Supplementary Information). Their predicted strengthening contribution is
ΔHVZr,ppt = 410 MPa. The peak-aging hardness increment (hardness of peak-aged alloy
subtracting hardness of as-fabricated alloy) for the binary Al-Zr alloy is ~500 MPa, near the
predicted precipitation strengthening contribution. The peak-aging hardness increment in the
ternary Al-Zr-X alloys ranges between 495-584 MPa; considering error bars, this is also within
error of the predicted precipitation strengthening contribution from L12-Al3Zr. Therefore, the
hardness increase during peak-aging is mostly due to precipitation of L12-Al3Zr.

We now consider the strengthening contributions from the ternary solute element, which may be
present either in solid solution or as precipitates. Since the peak-aging increment and radius of
L12-Al3Zr precipitates is similar among the ternary alloys, we assume that the ternary solute does
not affect the strengthening contribution from Zr. This is consistent with the observed similarity
of hardness increment between the binary Al-Zr (~500 MPa) and ternary Al-Zr-X alloys (495-
584 MPa) which suggests that these ternary solutes do not significantly influence the number
density or hardening response from L12-Al3Zr precipitates. While some differences in number
density are suggested by our APT results, the small sampling size and microstuctural
heterogeneity makes comparison of precipitate number density via this method difficult. Results
on similar cast Al-Zr based alloys in the literature containing these elements also do not suggest
a strong effect of these elements on either the hardening response or precipitation kinetics of
L12-Al3Zr [23-27]. Although some partitioning of the ternary solute is found inside the L12-
Al3Zr via APT (Fig. 6), solutes which significantly influence the precipitation kinetics (and
subsequent strengthening contribution) from L12-Al3Zr diffuse faster than Zr (e.g. Sc [54], Er
[55], Si [56]), unlike the slow-diffusing solutes studied here (Mn, Cr, V, Mo, W) which thus
most likely do not significantly influence the L12-Al3Zr hardening response.

Then, the strengthening contribution from the ternary solute element is estimated to be the
difference between the hardness of the ternary Al-Zr-X alloys and the binary Al-Zr alloy; this
difference Δ𝐻𝑉= 𝐻𝑉𝐴𝑙−𝑍𝑟−𝑋−𝐻𝑉𝐴𝑙−𝑍𝑟 is plotted in Fig. 11. In Fig. 11(a), we calculate Δ𝐻𝑉
for the peak-aged alloys, comparing to solid-solution strengthening models (equations from Ref.
[12] and calculations shown in Supplementary Information). The solid-solution strengtheningcontribution is assumed be independent of other strengthening mechanisms in the alloy,
including the precipitation strengthening contribution from L12-Al3Zr. APT measurements of
solute concentration in the α-Al matrix are used as model input. It can be seen that the solid-
solution strengthening model slightly underpredicts the increment Δ𝐻𝑉 in the Al-Zr-Mn, -Cr,
and -V alloys, and more drastically underpredicts this increment in the Al-Zr-Mo and -W alloys.
The additional strengthening may result from the binary Al-X precipitates present after L-PBF
fabrication in the Mo- and -W containing alloys. In Fig. 11(b), it is seen that this difference Δ𝐻𝑉
does not appear to significantly change as a function of aging time for all ternary alloys. This
suggests that the decrease in hardness after long-term exposure at 400°C is due to coarsening of
L12-Al3Zr, while the contribution from the ternary element remains near-constant.

For the Al-Zr-V, -Mo, and -W alloys, the ternary solute barely precipitates out of solution, and
the pre-existing precipitates from solidification barely coarsen, so Δ𝐻𝑉 is expected to be
constant. However, precipitation of Mn or Cr is observed at 400°C in the Al-Zr-Mn and -Cr
alloys. It has been reported that Al-Mn based alloys show poor age-hardening responses [57, 58]
due to a high activation energy for nucleation, while Mn is one of the most efficient solid-
solution strengthening elements per at.% in Al[1, 12]. The other solutes, Cr, V, Mo, and W, are
also predicted to be efficient solid-solution strengthening elements [1, 12]. The two solutes
which precipitate out during aging at 400°C, Mn and Cr, both form plate-like Al12Mn and Al7Cr
precipitates that are much coarser (on the order of 1 µm spacing, Fig. 9) than the L12-Al3Zr
nanoprecipitates (order of ~10 nm spacing, Fig. 5). Calculations are provided in Supplementary
Information comparing the strengthening contributions from either Mn or Cr in the peak-aged
(400°C/4h) and over-aged (400°C/1008h) conditions, which show that for the Al-Zr-Mn and Al-
Zr-Cr alloys the drop in solid solution strengthening contribution of Mn and Cr during aging is
barely balanced by a mild precipitation strengthening effect, consistent with the predicted stable
strengthening contributions from these elements for the aging times shown here. It should be
noted that for much longer aging times or even higher temperatures where precipitates continue
to coarsen, the Orowan strengthening contribution will decrease, resulting in decreased
strengthening from these elements.Figure 11. Hardness contribution from the ternary solute element plotted for (a) the peak-aged state (400°C/4h) with
comparison to solid-solution strengthening models, and (b) as a function of aging time at 400°C.




4.4. Creep resistance at 400°C

The creep resistance of the ternary Al-Zr-X alloys at 400°C is significantly improved over the
binary Al-Zr alloy (Fig. 10, Table S2), indicating that addition of these slow-diffusing solute
elements (Mn, Cr, V, Mo, W) improve creep resistance. Furthermore, even after 504 h exposure
at 400°C, the creep resistance of these alloys does not decrease, indicating excellent aging
resistance. These ternary alloys, containing primarily L12-Al3Zr nanoprecipitates and slow-

elements (Mn, Cr, V, Mo, W) improve creep resistance. Furthermore, even after 504 h exposure
at 400°C, the creep resistance of these alloys does not decrease, indicating excellent aging
resistance. These ternary alloys, containing primarily L12-Al3Zr nanoprecipitates and slow-
diffusing solutes, are comparable in their creep resistance to additively-manufactured Al alloys
containing much higher volume fractions (20-30%) of strengthening phases. Commercial
additively-manufactured alloys (e.g. Scalmalloy Al-Mg-Sc-Zr [46], Addalloy Al-Mg-Zr [59])
rely on L12 nanoprecipitates and Mg solutes for strengthening. Their high-temperature
mechanical properties may therefore be substantially improved by addition of these slow-
diffusing solute elements.

In the power-law creep regime of L12-strengthened Al alloys, creep deformation occurs by slow
climb of dislocations over L12-Al3Zr nano-precipitates, and fast glide in the Al matrix. It has
been previously observed that Mn in solid solution improves creep resistance in L12-
strengthened Al alloys [18-20]. The proposed mechanism is that slow-diffusing Mn solute atoms
exert further drag forces on dislocations as they climb over the L12 precipitates, slowing
dislocation climb and reducing creep deformation. Therefore, Cr, V, Mo, and W, which diffuse
even more sluggishly than Mn, likely provide strengthening by a similar mechanism.The creep resistance of these Al-Zr-X alloys does not appear to correlate with their solute
diffusivity. For instance, V is slower diffusing than Cr, but creep strain rates in the Al-Zr-V alloy
are slightly higher than that of Al-Zr-Cr, and neither the Al-Zr-Cr nor -V alloys are substantially
more creep-resistant than Al-Zr-Mn. Furthermore, Al-Zr-Mo and Al-Zr-W are more creep-
resistant than Al-Zr-V, but all three elements have approximately the same diffusivity in the Al
matrix. Previously for binary Al-X alloys, it was proposed that creep resistance increases with
decreasing solute diffusivity, and a mechanism controlled by solute diffusion at subgrain
boundaries was proposed to be rate-controlling [21, 22]. In our Al-Zr-X alloys, we do not
observe that creep resistance increases with decreasing solute diffusivity; this does not
necessarily contradict this previous model on binary Al-X alloys however as the introduction of
L12-Al3Zr precipitates changes the rate-controlling creep mechanism to dislocation climb over
precipitates. One possible explanation for this finding is that in alloys with fast-diffusing solutes,
solute atoms form atmospheres around the dislocation line that slow down dislocation motion,
while diffusing fast enough to be dragged along with the dislocation [60-62]. In the case of slow-
diffusing solutes such as Mn, the solutes diffuse much more slowly than the moving dislocations.
Thus, the dislocation velocity may not be controlled by the speed of the diffusing solute atoms,
but rather the strength of the drag stress imparted by solute atoms on the dislocation [62].

Calculating the drag stress from these solutes on dislocations as they climb over the L12-Al3Zr
precipitates is complex [18], but we elucidate here some factors which may explain the
difference in creep resistance imparted by these solutes, to guide future study. A model by
Sandstrom [62] was employed for Al-Mg alloys to calculate the drag stress imparted by Mg
atoms on dislocations and to predict strain rates as a function of stress. In this model, the drag
stress imparted by slow-diffusing solute atoms has been predicted to be controlled by their
interaction energy with the dislocation line and their concentration in the Al matrix. The largest
interaction energy contribution is from lattice misfit [62]; however it is thus unexpected that the
lattice misfits of Mo (-2.44%) and W (-2.68%) are smaller than those for Mn (-4.2%), Cr (-
3.83%), and V (-2.79%) [12]. Furthermore, the concentration of Mo and W in the Al matrix are
lower than those of the other solute elements, as determined via APT (Fig. 6, Table S1). In spite
of these observations, the Al-Zr-Mo and -W alloys are more creep resistant than the remaining
alloys. Another contributing factor to the solute-dislocation interaction energy is the modulus
mismatch. Modulus mismatch has been found to significantly contribute to solid-solution
strengthening at room temperature [63], and may also contribute to solid-solution strengthening
at high temperature during creep deformation [62, 64]. These modulus mismatch values are
available for Mn [65, 66], but not for the other solutes in this study to the best of the authors’
knowledge. The higher elastic moduli of Mo and W [63] may imply higher modulus mismatch
strengthening, but further study would be needed to clarify the contribution of modulus
mismatch between these solute elements and Al to the dislocation-solute interaction energy.
Previous DFT studies have calculated the dislocation-solute interaction strength and solute
concentration around edge dislocations for various solutes in Al (including Mn [18, 64]), but
modeling studies are needed for more insight into the mechanisms which govern creep
strengthening from slow-diffusing solute elements more generally, especially when precipitates
are present.5. Conclusions

In this study, Al-0.4Zr and five ternary Al-0.4Zr-1X (at.%) (X = Mn, Cr, V, Mo, and W) alloys
were prepared by laser powder-bed fusion, and their microstructural evolution and high-
temperature mechanical properties were studied. We conclude:

    1.  Extended supersaturation of Zr and X was achieved in all L-PBF processed alloys. No
       primary precipitates were visible in the Al-Zr-Mn and -Cr containing alloys, suggesting
       nearly all the ternary solute was retained in solid solution during fabrication. Some
       primary precipitates were visible in the Al-Zr-V, -Mo and -W alloys at the meltpool
       boundaries, consistent with the slower cooling rates at these boundaries allowing for
      some primary precipitation.

    2.  During thermal exposure at 400°C, the supersaturated elements in the solid solutions
        precipitate to form various phases (Al12Mn, Al7Cr, Al21V2, Al12Mo, and Al12W), both in
       the grain interiors and at grain boundaries for the Al-Zr-Mn and -Cr alloys, and only at
       grain boundaries in the Al-Zr-V, -Mo, and -W alloys. The precipitation process occurs at
        different rates which are consistent with the relative diffusivities of the ternary solutes:
    Mn precipitates from solution the fastest, followed by Cr, then V, Mo, and W, which
       mostly remain in solution even after three months at 400°C.

    3.  Addition of these ternary solutes improves the microhardness of all alloys during aging at
      400°C, and the ternary Al-Zr-X alloys are strengthened by L12-Al3Zr nanoprecipitates
      and the ternary solutes, either in solid solution or as micron-scale binary Al-X
        precipitates. The room-temperature strengthening contribution from the ternary X solute
       does not significantly change for up to three months exposure at 400°C.

    4. The compressive creep resistance at 400°C of all five ternary Al-Zr-X alloys is
        significantly higher than that of the binary Al-Zr alloy, indicating a strong creep
       strengthening effect from the slow-diffusing Mn, Cr, V, Mo, or W elements. The creep
        resistance of these alloys, containing only L12-Al3Zr precipitates and slow-diffusing
        solute atoms, is comparable to that of alloys containing much higher volume fractions of
       strengthening phases.Data availability - All data included in this study are available upon reasonable request by contact

Calculation of ternary solute strengthening contribution in over-aged alloys

We estimate the strengthening contributions in the Al-Zr-Mn and Al-Zr-Cr alloys in the
400°C/1008h aged state, summing contributions from the Mn/Cr solutes and the Al12Mn and
Al7Cr precipitates.

For the Mn/Cr solutes, we use the above Eq. S7 for solid solution strengthening. Direct
measurements of Mn concentration were not made in the 400°C/1008h aged Al-Zr-Mn alloy.
However, from the electrical resistivity curve for the Al-Zr-Mn solute, the resistivity has nearly
plateaued, and we estimate that the amount of Mn in solution is near its equilibrium value at
400°C, and estimate approximately 0.075±0.025 at.% in solution in solution. For the Al-Zr-Cr
alloy after 400°C/1008h aging, the resistivity contribution from Cr is nearly half its value in the
peak-aged state. The electrical resistivity can be modeled as a linear function of the solute
concentration [32]; therefore, we estimate that the concentration of Cr is approximately half its
original value, estimating a value of 0.3±0.1 at.% in solution.

For the Mn- and Cr-rich precipitates, we employ the Orowan strengthening equation, which is
appropriate for the size of the precipitates employed here. The volume fraction of Al12Mn
precipitates in the Al-Zr-Mn alloy was found via Rietveld analysis of the XRD patterns (using
GSAS-II) to be ~6 vol.%; that of Al7Cr was found to be ~5 vol.%. The equivalent spherical
radius of the Al12Mn and Al7Cr precipitates (taking the average of ~1000 precipitates each), was
found to be 103±20 nm and 91±20 nm, respectively.

strengthening and new precipitation strengthening). The predicted strengthening contribution
from the ternary solute has not significantly changed and may be within experimental error of

                        medium-entropy alloy produced by SLM. Therefore, the aim of this investigation was to
                          study the possibility of manufacturing a medium-entropy TRIP alloy of the Fe-Co-Ni-Cr-C
                         system using the SLM method, with a reasonable balance of strength and ductility at
                        low temperatures.

                                   2. Experimental

                           The powder for SLM was obtained by atomization of the vacuum induction melted
                             Fe65(CoNi)25Cr9.5C0.5 alloy using a US35 atomizer from ATO LAB. The rods (Ø10 mm)
                        were placed in a chamber that was purged with inert gas (argon). The obtained particles
                             of the alloy had a spherical shape with an average size of 35 µm (Figure 1a). The EDS
                            (Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy detector installed at a FEI Quanta 600 scanning
                             electron microscope (SEM)) maps suggest a uniform distribution of the elements within
                            the particles.
                      SLM of the alloy was carried out in an argon atmosphere using a 3D printer DMP Flex
                          200 (3D Systems Inc., Rock Hill, SC, USA); a 316L steel plate was used as a substrate. The
                   ﬂow rate of argon gas used as shielding gas was 5 L per minute. To improve the quality
                             of the workpieces, the direction of laser movement was changed by 67◦during fusion of
                          each subsequent layer [41] (Figure 1b); it should be noted that each laser beam track was
                           declined 67◦from the macroscopic scanning direction (SD). The distance between tracks
                       and the beam diameter were 50 µm and 70 µm, respectively.
                           The measured composition of the alloy (determined using optical emission spec-
                           troscopy or energy dispersive spectrometry (EDS); the percentages of C, O, and N were
                          determined by LECO thermal combustion analysis) is shown in Table 1.Materials 2023, 16, 3193                                                                                                         3 of 18

                               transverse direction, respectively; it should be noted that each laser beam track was declined 67◦

                                   3.1. Selection of the SLM Parameters

                           More than 50 attempts were made to establish the most appropriate parameters for the
                   SLM of the Fe65(CoNi)25Cr9.5C0.5 alloy. In the ﬁrst stage, monolayers of the alloy (measured

                          scan speed in the range of 400–2200 mm per second (Figure 3). It was found that at high
                       power values (>300 W) and low speeds (<400 mm/s), the SLM process was associated with

                           high speeds (>2000 mm/s) and low power (<150 W) resulted in a lack of adhesion with the
                              substrate and increased porosity of the layers, thereby suggesting incomplete melting of the

1. Introduction

   Since the 1950s, joint arthroplasty has entered clinical practice and has become widespread since the early 2000s owing to the
high-tech nature of this surgical intervention [1–3]. The materials from which modern joint endoprostheses are made have high
strength and good survival rate in the human body. Therefore, their service life is on average 15–20 years, and in many cases, patients
use them for up to 30 years [4–6]. When the endoprosthesis is worn out, it is replaced with a new one. According to patient obser­
vations, the following problems were identified in hip arthroplasty, in particular: there are massive zones of bone resorption around
the acetabular component of the endoprosthesis; threads on the cavity during the operation destroy the bone tissue that goes along
with osteolysis, ahead of the osseointegration of the acetabulum; and implant migration [7,8]. The main reason for such problems is
the simple topology of the endoprosthesis. Since, in normal cases, a computer selection of endoprostheses takes place in a data bank
with more than 40,000 prostheses, without taking into account patients’ physiological characteristics, i.e., the surgeon has to navigate
the operation, which also increases the time of prosthetics and is accompanied by corresponding risks [9–14].
   The development of new materials with required properties for implants of the human musculoskeletal system is extremely relevant
today [15,16]. An extremely large number of Ti beta-alloys have been created and studied to obtain a low modulus of elasticity [17].
Biomedical alloys have satisfactory mechanical properties and a record low modulus of elasticity. However, the existing beta alloys

of thermal and thermomechanical treatment, and impossibility of mechanical hardening significantly reduces the potential of these
alloys [20,21]. An alpha-beta titanium alloy Ti94Fe1Cu1Sn4, reported in our previous work [22], is an alternative candidate for a new
biomedical alloy. High mechanical and corrosion properties of this alloy have been also confirmed in another our previous study [23].
This paper proposes modes for obtaining spherical powder and selective laser melting (SLM) of samples from the resulting alloy
powder. In addition, it presents preliminary electrochemical comparative studies and the study of the morphology of the samples’
structure. The relevance of this work is predetermined by the practical obvious possibility of using this titanium alloy as a basis for
personalized implants created using additive technologies to replace old-generation orthopedic implants. Selective laser melting is a
modern method of the fabrication of fully dense parts with complex shapes. This method has several advantages due to its melting
peculiarities: the small size of the molten pool, short lifetime of the liquid state, and the rapid heating and cooling rates, which gives
effect on superfine microstructures formation after SLM. It should also be noted that this alloy does not contain alloying components
provoking allergic reactions, which will potentially have a positive effect on reducing revision operations. The investigation of the
Ti-based alloys with the close composition were published in the works [24–26], presented including the authors of the present work.

2. Materials and methods

   Pure metals with 99.9 % purity were used as raw materials for alloy preparation. An Arc 200 vacuum arc furnace (Arcast Inc.) with
a non-consumable tungsten electrode and copper crucible at an argon pressure of 3.5⋅104 Pa followed by purification using a Ti getter
was provided for the melting operation. Five times remelting and casting into a copper mold of 120 mm in length and 14 mm in

    It is known [39] that solidification hot tearing occurs in the late stages of solidification when the volume fraction of solid is above
85–95 %, and the solid phase is organized in a continuous network of grains. Resistance to hot tearing, as is known [39], is determined
by three factors: brittleness temperature range, plasticity in this temperature range, and strain growth rate [39]. In this regard, the
strain growth rate at a laser power of 250 W either contributes to sufficient relaxation of internal stresses or does not reach a value
preceding cracking. In this case, with a decrease in the scanning speed and, accordingly, an increase in Ev, the porosity decreases.
   The grain size significantly decreases after SLM according to the optimal fusion mode (Ev = 297.62 J/mm3) and is about 20–30 μm
(Fig. 5a), which coincides with the layer thickness in 3D printing. This is about 5 times less than for samples obtained by casting - the
grain size is about 100 μm (Fig. 5b), which should potentially improve mechanical properties without subsequent heat treatment.
   To determine the electrochemical behavior of the Ti94Fe1Cu1Sn4 alloy after SLM, potentiodynamic curves were obtained. Fig. 6
shows the electrochemical behavior in HBSS at 37 ◦C of the Ti94Fe1Cu1Sn4 alloy after optimal SLM treatment, and as a comparison:
Grade 1, Ti94Fe1Cu1Sn4 (as-cast). All samples are in the passive state and the value of the corrosion current density is low, as shown in
Table 2. Ti Grade 1, the Ti94Fe1Cu1Sn4 (as-cast) samples have a more negative corrosion potential (Fig. 6, Table 2), whereas the anodic
and cathodic curves of the Ti94Fe1Cu1Sn4 alloy sample after SLM have significant deviations from the cathodic to transpassive region. A
possible reason for this behavior is the different microsegregation of the alloy components in as-cast and SLM conditions.
   As is known, titanium alloys are not subject to electrochemical corrosion in neutral media due to the formation of a protective
passive film on the surface [40–43]. As a result of our comparative analysis with similar curves for Grade 1, Ti94Fe1Cu1Sn4 alloys, it
was found that due to the different protective ability of passive films on the studied samples, they have different inhibition of the
anodic process.
   As can be seen from Fig. 6 and Table 2, for Grade 1, as-cast Ti94Fe1Cu1Sn4, and the Ti94Fe1Cu1Sn4 alloy after SLM, different passive

   In accordance with the calculations of non-equilibrium solidification according to the Scheil-Gulliver model, the formation of Ti2Cu
phase precipitates by eutectic transition in a small amount is possible (Fig. 3a). The probable presence of the Ti2Cu phase determines
the unstable electrochemical behavior of the alloy after SLS in the Hanks solution (Fig. 6), as the Ti2Cu phase is an anodic structural
component with respect to the base alloy [45]. Its presence leads to the cyclic disinhibition of the anode process with a release of Cu2+
ions. It was previously established that the corrosion rate strongly depends on the morphology of the Ti2Cu phase [46]. Based on our
calculations (Fig. 3c), during homogenizing heat treatment at temperatures above 1000 ◦C, this phase should completely dissolve in
the β-Ti solid solution. Also, during the subsequent search for the mode, the second stage of heat treatment is needed, it is desirable to
achieve an optimal ratio of the α and β-Ti phases of 70:30 in terms of mechanical properties [22] without deteriorating the electro­
chemical behavior. At the same time, it is known that the presence of the Ti2Cu phase in binary titanium alloys of the Ti–Cu system has
an excellent effect on antibacterial properties [46,47]. Furthermore, with the acicular Ti2Cu phase, the antibacterial effect is two times
higher than with the presence of the finely dispersed Ti2Cu phase. The acicular precipitate has a higher Cu:Ti ratio, resulting in an
increased release of Cu2+ ions. In this regard, it is advisable in further

4. Conclusion

   This paper studied the potential possibility of selective laser melting of a new alpha-beta-titanium alloy Ti94Fe1Cu1Sn4, which has
high mechanical characteristics and does not contain components that cause allergic reactions [23], with the aim of further research to
manufacture personalized implants of a new generation. The spherical powders of the Ti94Fe1Cu1Sn4 alloy were obtained by plasma
atomization, from which the optimal regime for obtaining samples was determined by the SLM method. It was found that when the

Abstract

Refractory multi-principal element alloys offer high melting temperatures and
compositional flexibility for structural applications under extreme conditions. In the
Nb–Ti–Zr ternary system, Zr confers corrosion resistance and a low neutron capture
cross-section, while Nb stabilizes the body-centered cubic (BCC) phase across a
wide composition space, and Ti, the lightest constituent, lowers the alloy density.
Here we report the first additive manufacturing of Nb25Ti20Zr55 by laser powder bed
fusion (LPBF) and laser directed energy deposition (LDED) from a single prealloyed
powder. Both routes produced intact builds with sparse pores across much of the
processing window, with cracking confined to part of the LPBF range. Electron         Pre-proof
backscatter diffraction and X-ray diffraction indexed a predominantly body-centered
cubic microstructure at Zr contents of 50.4 to 55.5 at.% across both routes. Ti
evaporated preferentially, falling 9.5 at.% from the feedstock in LPBF, yet the BCC
phase was retained. The LPBF composition was uniform across the processing
window. The LDED composition varied with energy density and approached the
LPBF value only at the highest energy density. LPBF gave finer grains (96 µm) than
LDED (140 µm) at equivalent hardness (H = 2.73 to 2.90 GPa) and Young’s modulus
(E = 79 to 83 GPa).   Journal
Keywords: Refractory multi-principal element alloy; Laser powder bed fusion; Laser
directed energy deposition; Nb–Ti–Zr; Ultrasonic atomization; BCC phase

1  Introduction
Refractory metals and their alloys are attractive candidates for high-temperature
structural applications because of their high melting temperatures and their ability to
retain strength at temperatures exceeding the service limits of nickel-based
superalloys [1]. Among the refractory elements, Zr offers good corrosion resistance,
and a low thermal neutron capture cross-section, making Zr-based alloys the
standard cladding material in light water reactors [2], [3]. Despite decades of
development, broader deployment of refractory alloys has been constrained by
manufacturing difficulty: the high processing temperatures, limited room-temperature
ductility, and strong oxygen affinity of these materials impose severe constraints on
conventional fabrication routes [1]. For Zr-rich refractory alloy design,
multicomponent alloying provides a route to preserve the Zr-centered design
rationale while modifying phase stability and processability.



1Refractory multi-principal element alloys (RMPEAs) expand the accessible
compositional space by distributing multiple refractory elements in non-equiatomic
proportions, enabling independent alteration of phase stability, density, and
mechanical properties beyond the limits of conventional single-principal-element
refractory alloys [1].The Nb–Ti–Zr ternary system is particularly attractive because
Nb, Ti, and Zr exhibit extensive mutual solubility in the body-centered cubic (BCC)
phase at elevated temperatures, providing a broad non-equiatomic composition
space at comparatively low density [4], [5]. Although Nb is BCC at all temperatures,
Ti and Zr are hexagonal close-packed (HCP) at room temperature and transform to
BCC only above ≈882 °C and ≈863 °C, respectively [6], [7]. The BCC phase can
nevertheless be retained across selected ternary compositions through Nb additions,
which act as a BCC stabilizer [4], and through rapid solidification, which can suppress
equilibrium phase decomposition. Recent high-throughput screening by Lech et al.
using magnetron-sputtered thin films mapped this ternary space and established that
single-phase BCC stability requires Zr contents below 30.5 at.%, with oxygen acting
as a critical destabilizing factor [4]. The nominal composition Nb25Ti20Zr55,
investigated here, contains 55 at.% Zr and therefore lies outside the predicted single-
phase BCC stability field. In our previous work [8], the same composition formed
BCC after annealing and was identified as a promising candidate for laser-based
manufacturing, where single-track experiments demonstrated laser–material
compatibility. However, the transition from single-track screening to bulk additive
manufacturing (AM) has not yet been reported.

AM, and specifically laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), is attractive for refractory alloys
because it enables near-net-shape fabrication directly from powder feedstock whileimposing rapid solidification that canPre-proofreduce segregation length scales [9], [10].
However, LPBF of refractory systems remains challenging: large thermal gradients
generate residual stresses that promote cracking [11], and defects may arise from
solidification-related phenomena or from solid-state thermal cracking during
subsequent cooling [10], [11], [12]. The resulting defect populations are highly
system specific. Mooraj et al. demonstrated nearly defect-free LPBF of near-
equiatomic TiZrNbTa via in situ alloying of elemental powders and use of a
normalized processing diagram to identify a suitable processing window [13]. Other
refractory compositions, however, remain highly susceptible to cracking even after   Journal
parameter optimization [10], [14], confirming that processability is alloy specific.
Conventional refractory alloys such as C103 (Nb–10Hf–1Ti) have been processed by
LPBF to near-full density [15], yet no commercial end-product made of a refractory
high-entropy alloy has been reported to date [16]. Laser directed energy deposition
(LDED) provides a complementary additive route. Compared with LPBF, LDED
operates at lower cooling rates, larger melt pools, and lower spatial resolution, and it
accommodates feedstock variability through controlled powder flow into the melt pool
[9], [17], [18], [19]. Keyhole porosity and balling are melt pool instabilities associated
with the high beam intensities and scan speeds typical of LPBF [9], [18], whereas
LDED is more susceptible to dilution and macro-segregation [18]. LPBF and LDED
impose different cooling rat

## 2. chmielewska2026asinglepowderstrategy pages 3-6 (Context ID: pqac-00000068)

lloys such as C103 (Nb–10Hf–1Ti) have been processed by
LPBF to near-full density [15], yet no commercial end-product made of a refractory
high-entropy alloy has been reported to date [16]. Laser directed energy deposition
(LDED) provides a complementary additive route. Compared with LPBF, LDED
operates at lower cooling rates, larger melt pools, and lower spatial resolution, and it
accommodates feedstock variability through controlled powder flow into the melt pool
[9], [17], [18], [19]. Keyhole porosity and balling are melt pool instabilities associated
with the high beam intensities and scan speeds typical of LPBF [9], [18], whereas
LDED is more susceptible to dilution and macro-segregation [18]. LPBF and LDED
impose different cooling rates, melt pool geometries, and mass transfer conditions.
The two routes may therefore produce different composition retention and
microstructural responses for the same alloy. Laser cladding of NbTiZr coatings on Zr
substrates has been reported [20], and LDED has been demonstrated for the related
quinary TiZrNbHfTa system [21]. However, bulk consolidation of the ternary Nb–Ti–Zr
alloy from the same prealloyed powder by both LPBF and LDED has not been
reported.


2Suitable powder feedstock is a further prerequisite for reliable laser-based AM. In
LPBF, powder spreading and recoating govern layer formation, whereas in LDED,
stable powder delivery and carrier gas transport govern material feeding into the melt
pool. Both routes therefore require chemically homogeneous powder with suitable
particle size distribution (PSD), morphology, and flowability [9], [16]. For
multicomponent refractory alloys, prealloyed powder is preferable when comparing
process routes because incomplete in situ alloying and local compositional
heterogeneity in blended elemental feedstock can obscure composition retention,
phase retention, and visible cracking responses [1], [13]. Using one prealloyed
powder for both LPBF and LDED minimizes feedstock variability, so that differences
between routes can be interpreted primarily in terms of processing conditions.
Ultrasonic atomization is well suited for this purpose because it produces spherical,
satellite-free powder with a controllable PSD [22]. Ultrasonically atomized metal
powder has been reported to exhibit good flowability [23], supporting its relevance for
powder spreading in LPBF and powder feeding in LDED [9], [16].

The present work investigates the AM of nominal Nb25Ti20Zr55 using two
complementary laser-based routes: LPBF and LDED. Prealloyed powder produced
by ultrasonic atomization was characterized for morphology, chemistry, and particle
size distribution, then used as feedstock for parametric processing trials in both LPBF
and LDED. Laser power and scan speed were varied at constant hatch spacing and
layer thickness for each process, and the resulting builds were assessed in
representative conditions for geometric integrity, visible cracking, composition
retention, phase constitution, and grain structure. Modified volumetric energy density
is used as a comparative descriptor to organize the LPBF and LDED parameterspaces. The study evaluates how processPre-proofroute affects composition retention, phase
constitution, and grain structure in a Zr-rich RMPEA processed from the same
prealloyed powder.

2  Materials and Methods
2.1  Feedstock material fabrication by ultrasonic atomization
Alloyed powder was produced by ultrasonic atomization using a rePOWDER system
(Amazemet Ltd., Warsaw, Poland). Nb, Ti, and Zr supplied as slugs of purity   Journal≥99.95% and pellets were melted to form a homogeneous ingot. Physical properties
of the constituent elements are listed in Table 1. The nominal target composition was
Nb25Ti20Zr55 (at.%). The ingot was fed onto a 40 kHz titanium–zirconium–
molybdenum (TZM) sonotrode and remelted by a plasma torch. Ultrasonic vibrations
fragmented the molten metal into droplets that solidified into spherical powder
particles during free fall inside the atomization chamber under argon flow (99.999%).
After atomization, the powder was sieved, and the fraction below 100 µm was used
for subsequent LPBF and LDED processing and feedstock characterization.

32.2  Additive manufacturing by LPBF and LDED
Cubic specimens were fabricated on a Ti-6Al-4V substrate. LPBF specimens had a
nominal edge length of 4 mm; LDED specimens had a nominal edge length of 6 mm.

For LPBF, a Sisma MySint100 (Sisma S.p.A., Italy) system was used. It is equipped
with a 200 W fiber laser operating at 1070 nm, with a nominal spot diameter (dL) of
55 µm and a Gaussian intensity distribution. Argon (99.999% purity) served as
shielding gas, and the oxygen level in the chamber was kept below 100 ppm. A
constant layer thickness of 30 µm and a hatch spacing of 100 µm were applied for all
builds.

LDED experiments were carried out on an MX-Lab system (InssTek Inc., Republic of
Korea) equipped with a 500 W fiber laser at 1070 nm, with a larger nominal spot
diameter of 400 µm and a Gaussian intensity distribution. The nominal nozzle to
surface distance was 9 mm, the shielding-gas flow rate was 8 L min-1, and argon
(99.999% purity) served as both shielding and powder carrier gas. The powder feed
rate was set to 0.9 g min-1. A constant layer thickness of 150 µm and a hatch spacing
of 300 µm were used. The dwell time between successive layers was set to 3.5 sec.


In both processes, a bidirectional scanning strategy with a 90° rotation between
successive layers was applied. The nominal laser power (PL) and scan velocity (vL)
were varied, while layer thickness (tp) and hatch spacing (h) were kept constant. For
LPBF, the parameter ranges were 100 to 175 W and 400 to 1000 mm s-1. For LDED,         Pre-proofthey were 125 to 225 W and 600 to 1080 mm min-1. Process parameters are listed in
Table 2.

2.3  Microstructural characterization
Powder, LPBF, and LDED specimens were embedded in epoxy, ground with SiC
paper to 1000 grit, polished with 3 µm diamond suspension, and finished with 20 nm
colloidal silica. LPBF and LDED cross sections were prepared as single longitudinal
sections containing the build direction.





5Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy
(EDS) were performed on a Mira3 (Tescan, Brno, Czech Republic) with an Apollo X
detector (EDAX, Mahwah, NJ, USA)at 30 kV. Elemental maps were used to assess
compositional homogeneity in both powder and additively manufactured material.
Powder compositions are reported as atomic-number, absorption, and fluorescence
(ZAF)-corrected means of six-point analyses of particle cross-sections. The reported
uncertainty is the 1σ SmartQuant Error% returned by the software. LPBF and LDED
compositions are means over multiple areas or line scans per condition, with
uncertainties as standard deviations. Nb Lα and Zr Lα peak overlap was deconvolved
within the ZAF-corrected SmartQuant routine.

Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) was performed on a Tescan Mira SEM
equipped with an EDAX DigiView camera, acquired at 30 kV with a 1 µm step size,
and analyzed using EDAX OIM Analysis 7.3 software. Grain boundaries were defined
by a 15° misorientation threshold.

X-ray diffraction maps were collected on the cross sections of LPBF and LDED using
the custom-built Swissmapper instrument at Empa, on a regular grid with 500 µm
spacing. For each specimen an average diffraction pattern was calculated from all
measurement positions lying well inside the specimen boundary, comprising at least
28 positions. The diffractometer operates in fixed-angle reflection geometry with an
incidence angle of 17.5° and an exposure time of 20 s per position. The incident Cu
Kα beam (50 kV, 1 mA) was focused to a spot size of 150 µm using ASTIX optics
(AXO DRESDEN GmbH), giving a sample footprint of approximately 270 µm
equivalent circular diameter. Patterns were recorded on a stationary EIGER2 1M two-
dimensional detector (Dectris AG) covering a 2θ range of 30 to 120°. The         Pre-proof
experimental geometry was calibrated in pyFAI using LaB6 standard reference
material (NIST SRM 660c). Raw two-dimensional images were azimuthally integrated
into one-dimensional profiles using 1000 bins in 2θ and 1000 bins in the azimuthal
angle χ, giving a 2θ resolution of approximately 0.095°.

Grain size is reported as the area-weighted mean equivalent circle diameter (ECD)
from the OIM Analysis grain reconstruction, with edge grains excluded. Grain
elongation was quantified separately by a directional linear intercept method (Heyn,
ASTM E112 [25]) on the reconstructed boundary maps, using parallel and transverse   Journal
test lines at a nominal 10 µm spacing. The aspect ratio AR = L∥/L⊥ is the ratio of
mean intercept lengths parallel and transverse to the build direction, so AR > 1
indicates elongation along the build direction, edge grains were included in the
intercept count.

The PSD was measured by laser diffraction on a Mastersizer 3000+ Pro (Malvern
Panalytical, Malvern, UK; range 0.1 to 2500 µm) in dry dispersion with the Aero S
adapter. Particle size is the volume-equivalent spherical diameter, reported as the
D10, D50, and D90 percentiles of the cumulative volume distribution.

Nanoindentation was performed using a ZHN nanoindenter (ZwickRoell, Ulm,
Germany) equipped with a Berkovich diamond tip (Synton MDP, Switzerland) and
operated in load-controlled mode using a fast hardness protocol without continuous
stiffness measurement. Before testing, the tip area function was calibrated on a fused
silica reference. A maximum load of 5 mN was applied, with loading and unloading
rates of 10 mN s-1 and a dwell time of 1 s at maximum load. Indents were spaced
5 µm apart and arranged in line scans spanning the top to the bottom of each



6sample. Three line scans were acquired per sample, and sample preparation
followed the metallographic procedure described above for microstructural analysis.
1000 µm measured from the deposit surface was retained for bulk property
extraction. Hardness (H) and reduced elastic modulus (Er) were determined from the
load-displacement data using the Oliver–Pharr method [26]. Per-row outliers were
rejected by retaining values within the kernel-density-estimated peak ± 2σ at the half
maximum of each row, and H and Er were then averaged across the three line scans
at each indent position. Young's modulus E was computed from Er using a single
sample Poisson's ratio νs = 0.34, which lies within the ν = 0.30 to 0.38 range reported
for Nb, Ti, and Zr [27], together with the diamond indenter constants Ei = 1141 GPa
and νi = 0.07.

3.1  Feedstock characterization
SEM imaging in Figure 2 revealed that the powder consisted predominantly of
spherical particles with clean external surfaces. No pronounced satellites,
agglomerates, or severely irregular particles were observed in the analyzed fraction.
At higher magnification, the particle surfaces exhibited a fine cellular solidification

(+2.5 ± 1.5 at.%) and depleted in Zr (−7.0 ± 0.6 at.%).

Novel titanium‑based sulfur‑containing BMG for PBF‑LB/M

Hanna Schönrath1     · Jan Wegner1,2 · Maximilian Frey3 · Martin A. Schroer2,4 · Xueze Jin5 ·
María Teresa Pérez‑Prado6 · Ralf Busch3 · Stefan Kleszczynski1,2


Received: 29 April 2024 / Accepted: 7 May 2024 / Published online: 25 May 2024
© The Author(s) 2024

Abstract
This paper investigates the additive manufacturing route for a novel glass-forming titanium-based sulfur-containing alloy of
the composition Ti60Zr15Cu17S8 . This system is a promising candidate for medical devices since the lack of toxic components
is combined with a high corrosion resistance and strength. Preliminary experiments and simulations show a general
processability of bulk material by powder bed fusion technologies. TEM and XRD reveal an amorphous microstructure of
laser-treated surfaces. Ultrasonic atomization is used to fabricate a flowable powder feed stock with spherical morphology and
crystalline microstructure, which is suitable for processing in powder bed fusion. Correlations between detected crystalline
phase formations and melt pool dynamics are revealed by SEM and EDX. It is shown that bulk samples with a high relative
density and partially crystalline microstructure can be manufactured.

 ORIGINAL ARTICLE


Recycling of Ti-15Mo and Ti-13Nb-13Zr alloys and their use in additive
manufacturing

Eliška Galčíková1     · Jan Krčil1 · Vladimír Mára1 · Lucie Pilsová1 · Jana Sobotová1 · Zdeněk Míchal2 · Dalibor Vojtěch3 ·
Jiří Režnar4


Received: 3 December 2025 / Accepted: 20 February 2026 / Published online: 14 March 2026
© The Author(s) 2026

Abstract
Recycling of titanium alloys represents a modern and economically attractive processing route, as it enables a significant
reduction in production costs associated with the high price of titanium. However, the properties of recycled β-titanium
alloys have not yet been sufficiently investigated in the scientific literature, and their potential for processing by additive
manufacturing technologies remains largely unexplored. This study focuses on evaluating the recycling of Ti-15Mo and
Ti-13Nb-13Zr alloys using the horizontal plasma arc melting (HPAM) method and further examines subsequent process­
ing steps, including hot working to the required shape for atomisation and subsequent powder processing via the LPBF
technique. In all technological stages, the microstructure was characterised, chemical analysis was performed, and, where
applicable, mechanical properties were evaluated. The results demonstrate that recycling of the investigated alloys is
feasible, as is their subsequent processing up to the production of additively manufactured specimens. Nevertheless, strict
control of the oxygen content is critical for both alloys, as the current levels exceed the limits specified by the relevant
standards. At such elevated oxygen concentrations, the alloys are unsuitable for biomedical applications; however, their
use in structural applications remains realistic, particularly considering the production cost reduction achieved through
the implementation of recycling.

Keywords  Ti-15Mo · Ti-13Nb-13Zr · Recycling process · Laser powder bed fusion
